articles.content: Looking for a different day? I began by threading together CHESS, GO, OTHELLO and STRATEGO. I'd never heard of STRATEGO, although the clue was in the name — but OTHELLO is a game I’ve grown up with and developed a winning strategy for (basically go for the corners), so this was an easy set. CUTTING EDGE and LOCATIONS FOR AN INSTITUTION both seemed far too easy, making this the one game of the week without any traps. Yesterday's NYT Connections answers (Friday, November 13, 2026, game #1251) YELLOW: USE THE INTERNET: BROWSE, SCROLL, SEARCH, SURF GREEN: MEDIA ATTENTION: COVERAGE, EXPOSURE, PRESS, PUBLICITY BLUE: THINGS THAT ARE TOWED: BARGE, GLIDER, TRAILER, WATER SKIER PURPLE: BRAIN ____: FREEZE, TEASER, TRUST, WAVES What is NYT Connections? NYT Connections is one of several increasingly popular word games made by the New York Times. It challenges you to find groups of four items that share something in common, and each group has a different difficulty level: green is easy, yellow a little harder, blue often quite tough and purple usually very difficult. On the plus side, you don't technically need to solve the final one, as you'll be able to answer that one by a process of elimination. What's more, you can make up to four mistakes, which gives you a little bit of breathing room. It's a little more involved than something like Wordle, however, and there are plenty of opportunities for the game to trip you up with tricks. articles.title: Amazon has a plan to index the world’s online shopping data
articles.content: Amazon has plans to build a vault of data on every product sold anywhere on the internet, even products Amazon doesn't sell, and make the information available through its own site, according to Reuters . The project, called the "World Product Graph," is meant to make it less likely that shoppers leave Amazon to do their product research on Reddit or Google, and make it more likely shoppers end up at Amazon even if they're searching for a product sold elsewhere. The same goes for AI agents - if Amazon has the largest stockpile of shopping data, AI agents may rely on its index of products over others, so even people shopping with bots will end … Read the full story at The Verge.
articles.author: Stevie Bonifield

This data will also be beneficial for AI agents, as they may prefer Amazon's extensive product index.

articles.title: Production MLOps at GS Caltex with Amazon SageMaker Canvas, part 1
articles.content: GS Caltex uses Amazon SageMaker Canvas and Amazon SageMaker Pipelines to connect process engineers’ models to production workflows. The South Korean energy and chemical company divides model development and operations between engineers with complementary skills. Process engineers build and validate models in SageMaker Canvas without writing code, drawing on their process knowledge. Machine learning (ML) engineers configure SageMaker Pipelines workflows for deployment and scheduled inference. Moving assets from SageMaker Canvas into SageMaker Pipelines still required integration work. ML engineers had to set data paths for production, supply the model configuration, and connect preprocessing and inference jobs. GS Caltex automated this handoff while reusing the assets created in SageMaker Canvas. GS Caltex reports that its ML engineers now deploy models within a few hours, compared with about a week before. The company runs batch inference every 30 minutes, reducing the need for continuously running endpoints. GS Caltex reports that this has meaningfully lowered its inference costs. This post explains how GS Caltex connects SageMaker Canvas to SageMaker Pipelines and reuses validated preprocessing flows and models in production. Solution overview The machine learning operations (MLOps) workflow has two paths: preparing a new model version for deployment, and running batch inference with the deployed model. From a validated model to a repeatable workflow You can use SageMaker Canvas to prepare data visually, build models, and generate batch predictions. You can also register validated models in Amazon SageMaker Model Registry from SageMaker Canvas. GS Caltex built a separate handoff process to turn these assets into executable SageMaker Pipelines steps. Process engineers understand the variables and data behind a process and assess whether a model’s predictions are useful. ML engineers turn the resulting assets into production jobs and manage model versions and execution history. Area What is prepared in SageMaker Canvas What is managed in the production workflow Data preparation A preprocessing flow built with Data Wrangler Preprocessing jobs in Amazon SageMaker Processing Model development A trained model and evaluation results Model versions and approval status in Model Registry Prediction Validation of model predictions Batch inference every 30 minutes using an approved model Operations Development and validation of individual models Step execution history, stored results, and failure handling Reference architecture The following diagram shows how process engineers hand off SageMaker Canvas assets to ML engineers for deployment and scheduled inference. ML engineers use Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) for preprocessing flows and Model Registry for model versions, then schedule pipeline runs through Amazon EventBridge. Figure 1: SageMaker Canvas assets connected to a SageMaker Pipelines workflow for scheduled batch inference ML engineers receive the preprocessing flow and model from SageMaker Canvas and review the data formats and prediction results. After that review, they approve the model in Model Registry and deploy it. This preparation takes place when a new model version is deployed. Subsequent inference runs reuse the deployed model. Amazon EventBridge starts each scheduled run. SageMaker Pipelines prepares the input data from Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), runs preprocessing and SageMaker Batch Transform , and stores the results in S3. ML engineers can inspect step status and Amazon CloudWatch logs to monitor the workflow. The production pipeline reuses the preprocessing logic and trained model created in SageMaker Canvas. ML engineers configure the input and output paths, set the order of execution, and write the code that connects approval and scheduling to the workflow. articles.title: FAA orders third nationwide ground stop in its history
articles.content: On Friday afternoon, days after expanding use of an AI tool , the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop, halting departures from all US airports. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy announced the ground stop on X , citing a "communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers." Duffy promised updates as more information is known and said FAA staff were troubleshooting the problem. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that the ground stop was not prompted by a security threat. "This is a telecommunications outage out of the FAA. Out of an abundance of caution, we have grounded all of the flights," Mullin said . "There's no indication as of yet that this is a nefarious attack against us." Mullin said the FAA would handle incoming international flights on a case-by-case basis. Read full article Comments

articles.title: DHS chief sees no link between Microsoft outage and FAA ground stop, doesn’t rule out AI
articles.content: Updated with Microsoft statement. The nationwide ground stop that halted U.S. departures Friday afternoon has no apparent connection to the Microsoft 365 outage that began a day earlier, but a link to the FAA’s new AI traffic-planning tool can’t be ruled out yet, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at a news conference. Asked whether the Microsoft outage and the FAA failure were a coincidence, Mullin said, “I don’t see any reason to connect those two at all. Those are separate issues.” Microsoft also said it has no indication that the FAA ground stop is related to its service disruption, according to a statement from a company spokesperson. Mullin described the problem as a telecommunications outage affecting the FAA’s air traffic control centers, though he said the cause isn’t yet known. “This isn’t another 9/11. I just can’t repeat that enough,” he said. The FAA said Tuesday it was expanding its AI system, known as SMART, to the airspace managed by all 22 of its en route air traffic control centers. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday’s communications problem affected all of those centers, though Mullin said two areas in the U.S. could still communicate normally. The agency describes SMART as a cloud-based system that pulls in about 200 data streams, including weather, flight paths and controller staffing, to recommend flight schedules and routes. FAA specialists review its recommendations, and local facilities decide whether to act on them. Asked about a possible link between the outage and the new system, Mullin said, “We’re looking at that,” adding that DHS was examining it through its Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). In response to a separate question about whether the problem could be AI-related, Mullin first corrected the reporter, saying, “We call it SI around here,” a reference to President Trump’s preferred term, “super intelligence.” He then added, “You just can’t rule out anything at this point. We’re going through that process, and we’re going to find out what happened.” SMART is part of a 12-year, $875 million FAA contract with Boston-based Air Space Intelligence that also covers a broader traffic flow management platform. Lawmakers asked the FAA in October to pause use of the tool in the Washington area. Air Space Intelligence denied any connection in a post on X. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said. Mullin also declined to rule out a cyberattack, saying, “We’re not ruling out anything at this point.” He said officials had seen no indication of a malicious attack. The FAA halted departures nationwide shortly before 1 p.m. Pacific. Flights already in the air could land, and inbound international flights were handled case by case. There are currently 3,100 airborne aircraft bound for US airports amid nationwide ground stop. No additional aircraft are taking off at this time. pic.twitter.com/GGqfb8QXhP — Flightradar24 (@flightradar24) November 13, 2026 Mullin said controllers can still communicate “at certain levels,” but the problem has “overwhelmed some of the systems we have.” He said restoring normal operations “isn’t going to just be resolved and turned around within the hour.” The outages involved air traffic control radars as well as radio frequencies going out at the same time, CNN’s Rene Marsh reported , citing an aviation source familiar with what controllers were dealing with. Controllers had no clarity on the cause, the source said. It’s the second nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11 attacks, after a January 2023 failure of the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions system. FlightAware counted nearly 7,000 flights delayed or canceled as of Friday afternoon. The Microsoft outage started Thursday morning in Exchange Online, the service that runs Outlook email for businesses, and spread to Teams calendars, Copilot and SharePoint,…

articles.title: Lego's BrickLink Marketplace Back Online After Week-Long Outage Caused By 'Cyber Incident'
articles.content: LEGO's BrickLink marketplace is back online after a week-long outage caused by what the company described as a "cyber incident," during which an unauthorized third party accessed some user data. Details about exactly what data was accessed remain unclear. The site went offline on November 5 and remained unavailable until November 12, preventing users from buying or selling LEGO sets and parts during the busy holiday shopping season. According to Brick Fanatics, LEGO initially described the outage as "necessary work" before confirming that the platform had suffered a security incident. In an email to users, LEGO acknowledged that "some of the information associated with your account was accessed and disclosed by an unauthorized party," including potentially usernames and IP addresses. However, the company insisted that "your password, postal address, and financial information were not disclosed." Those assurances have since come under scrutiny following reports of convincing phishing emails containing detailed personal and purchase information. The outage also dealt a significant blow to independent sellers who rely on BrickLink for income. Simon Webster, who operates stores on both BrickLink and rival marketplace Brick Owl, reported that his overall sales revenue fell 52% over a four-day period, even as sales through Brick Owl rose 79%. "Their comms are amateur at the best of times, but surely they should be able to send an email to let sellers and buyers alike know what is happening and what they're doing to rectify it," Webster said. "But no, we're all left in the dark." The incident has renewed concerns about BrickLink's aging infrastructure. Founded in 2000 and acquired by LEGO in 2019, the marketplace reportedly runs on a complex collection of interconnected systems that makes modernization difficult. The Brick Fanatics report questions whether the 25-year-old platform remains fit for purpose and whether prolonged outages and security concerns could push sellers toward competing marketplaces like Brick Owl. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.author: BeauHD

articles.title: 007 First Light composers explain how they honoured the ‘legacy’ sound of Bond, while leaving ‘plenty of room for more modern elements’
articles.content: 007 First Light composers Joe Henson and Alexis Smith explain how they captured the "legacy" of Bond Henson says, "There was never really a question about how we would attack the project" Smith says the music "must make the player feel like they are inhabiting the universe of James Bond" The composers for 007 First Light 's soundtrack have shared how they combined their musical experience to capture the classic James Bond "legacy." In an interview with TechRadar Gaming, musical duo The Flight, aka Joe Henson and Alexis Smith, explained how they adapted their signature synth and acoustic hybrid sounds to fit the traditional Bond style, with the former saying, "This score feels like the culmination of all the work we have done over the past decade or so." "Everything we have learned in this time has given us the tools we required to compose our score for First Light ," Henson said. "There was never really a question about how we would attack the project; our sound is what we do, and we were confident that it would marry with the more ‘legacy’ elements of Bond." Smith added that the word "legacy" meant the inclusion of Brass, strings, orchestral, and jazz elements were also important to include, saying, "While it’s true that this is probably the score of ours that has gone furthest in that direction, there was still plenty of room for more modern elements." "That’s one of the great things about the James Bond franchise, and especially the music – it moves with the times, always changing, always balancing the classic sounds with a current edge," Henson said. The James Bond theme is one of the most recognizable pieces of cinema music of all time, so the composers needed to retain that cultural significance while also incorporating their own spin to make a sound that was "original" for the First Light . When asked what characteristics the pair felt were vital, Smith said the music "must make the player feel like they are inhabiting the universe of James Bond." "It has to have spy craft, intrigue, action and romance," he said. "I can’t think of any other projects we’ve done that manage to combine those four things!" Henson continued, saying, "There's also a Bond Sound. Even as we’re holding back on the themes that everyone knows, there is still a Sound . It’s hard to describe, but I think we began to develop an instinctive feel for when something was Bond or not. It isn’t just the iconic motifs; it’s a very particular use of brass and strings, guitars and other instruments." Smith added, "Maybe it’s growing up in 1980s Britain and watching the movies on the sofa with our dads every Sunday, but we seemed to know instantly whether something sounded Bond enough or not!" The Flight’s soundtrack for 007 First Light is nominated in the Best Original Video Game Score category at the Ivors Composer Awards , which are taking place at Grosvenor House in London on November 17, 2026.
articles.author: Demi Williams

articles.title: FAA grounds all US flights due to 'telecommunication outage' — officials say ' no indication...that this was a nefarious attack,' but they can't rule out a cyberattack yet
articles.content: For only the third time in 25 years, the FAA has called a ground stop for all air traffic in the US. US officials said a telecommunications issue has hampered Air Traffic Control Centers across the US and their ability to communicate with planes in the air. Around 4:30PM ET, the FAA issued, according to ABC News, an extraordinary alert to pilots that reads in part: "Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety. Attention all aircraft operators. By order of the Federal Aviation Command Center, all airports are ground stopped." While US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has yet to issue a public statement (beyond the initial announcement of the ground stop), Department of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told reporters that this grounding, or the cause of it, "is not a threat to the US," and added it was a telecommunications outage. He did not detail the exact affected technology, though, when asked about the coincidence of the massive Microsoft Outlook outage yesterday and this today, Mullin said, "I don't see any reason to connect those two at all." A Microsoft X account also made the same point , writing, "We have no indication that the FAA’s nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services." Future Future On the possibility that this is a cyberattack, Mullin said they were not ruling anything out and "As we investigate what caused this, we always have to assume — as many cyberattacks take place —we make that assumption, but that's not known." The ongoing grounding comes a day after the FAA made an announcement of its AI-backed SMART system (Strategic Management of Airspace Routing Trajectories) to more airports . However, that rollout started back in September. So any connection there would be conjecture. There was a moment, though, when someone asked Mullin about that AI system, and Mullin quipped, "We call it 'SI' around here." As of now, air traffic control systems around the country are managing landings on what Mullin called "a case-by-case basis." (Image credit: Future) We started tracking the skies over the US via Flightradar24 more than an hour ago, and its depiction of in-flight planes and the direction they're heading over the last hour or so is remarkable. It went from being a fairly normal flight day to a visually chaotic race back home. Flights that may have taken off appear to have been rerouted back to their nearest airports. While JetBlue and American Airlines websites make no mention of the FAA grounding, Delta has a banner at the top of its site and recommends that everyone check their Delta App for their flight status. For now, Mullin said pilots and air traffic controllers can communicate "at certain levels, but they have some " overwhelmed" communication systems. Online pundits, including pilots and aviation experts, think there may be a fairly pedestrian issue. Scott Manley, a YouTube science expert and pilot, wrote on X : "It sounds to me like the ATC outage is limiting the ability for enroute centers to communicate with each other. As aircraft move across the country, they get handed off from one controller to the next, and your flight information is handed between controllers in a separate channel." Whatever the cause, it may take a day or more to untangle this mess. Did you know TechRadar now has membership? articles.title: RevOps Is Quietly Becoming an Engineering Job
articles.content: Over the last two weeks, I've written here about a calendar table that knows November 1 has 25 hours, a customer health score that barely beats a coin flip, a 1961 warehouse formula that finds dead deals in a CRM, a Slack report that checks its own numbers before it posts, an exam for AI agents, a macOS job that died because of where it kept its log file, and why 3x pipeline coverage is a guess. My title is Head of Revenue Operations. Very little of that shows up in a RevOps job description. I started in supply chain, moved into revenue operations, and taught myself SQL along the way. For most of that time, the job looked the way people describe it: own the CRM, build the reports, run the forecast, keep sales and finance looking at the same numbers. That's still the job. But the way it gets done has changed, and I think it's changing faster than the job descriptions. What Changed? Two things, mostly. The data moved into the warehouse. RevOps used to live inside the CRM and its report builder. Now the numbers that matter, from billing, product usage, payments, and the CRM itself, land in Snowflake or BigQuery. The person who reconciles them needs SQL, not a report wizard. Writing code got cheap. An AI coding agent will write the script that syncs the CRM, builds the workbook, or posts the report in minutes. That's the real shift. When code is cheap, more of RevOps becomes code, and someone has to run it. Running it is the part that didn't get cheaper. A script is easy. A script that runs at 7:45 every morning for two years, survives a laptop update, posts nothing when the data is wrong, and tells someone when it didn't run at all: that's operations engineering. And it's increasingly a RevOps problem, because the scripts are about revenue and nobody else owns them. What I'd learn now. If you work in RevOps, sales ops, or finance ops and you're wondering where to invest, here's my list, roughly in order of how often each one has saved me. SQL, properly. Not just SELECT and GROUP BY. Grain, joins that duplicate rows, window functions, time zones. Most wrong numbers I've chased came down to a join or a day boundary. ( These six Snowflake patterns cover the ones I reach for every week.) One scheduler, and how it fails. cron, launchd, GitHub Actions, Airflow. Pick the one you'll actually use and learn what it does when things go wrong. Every scheduler has a way to fail silently. Know yours. Version control for anything that produces a number. If it ends up in front of a CFO, it goes in git. "Which version of the query made that slide?" should have an answer. Testing numbers, not just code. Reconciliations, check cells, golden questions with known answers. Code that runs is not code that's right. Staging and promotion. Somewhere to break things that isn't production, and a deliberate step between the two. Writing definitions down. Every metric needs a written definition that sales and finance have both agreed to. It's the least technical item on this list, and the one that prevents the most arguments. Working with AI agents. Give them a sandbox, an exam, and a short list of things they're never allowed to touch. Then let them do a lot of the typing. What not to become The risk in all of this is that RevOps turns into a shadow data engineering team: pipelines nobody else understands, a dozen scheduled jobs on one laptop, and a single person who knows how any of it works. That version is worse than not automating at all. So draw a line. Data engineering owns the platform: ingestion, the warehouse, the infrastructure everyone shares. RevOps owns the business logic and the last mile: the definitions, the reconciliations, the reports, and the small automations that move revenue numbers to the people who use them. And give the last mile an exit. When a RevOps automation becomes important enough that its failure would hurt the company, it graduates to the platform, with real monitoring, an owner on call, and a second person who understands…

articles.title: All US flights grounded by FAA
articles.content: The US Federal Aviation Administration on Friday issued an advisory that prevents the takeoff of flights in US airspace, creating chaos for travelers and airports. "The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in a statement. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them." A spokesperson at the FAA press office reached by phone said he was unable to provide further information. And an email response from the agency repeated Duffy's statement. The FAA ATCSCC advisory halts departing flights and says international flights will be dealt with individually. The notice says, "Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety. Attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped. All departing traffic should remain stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis." Doug Yakel, public information officer for San Francisco International Airport, said, "FAA confirms nationwide ground stop, other reporting indicates a communications issue between Air Route Traffic Control Centers (ARTCCs). Aircraft already enroute to SFO still landing here but departing aircraft not taking off right now." An update issued at 2:02 pm PT described the problem as "a temporary telecommunications outage." The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) is managed by L3Harris. The network provides secure communication between more than 4,400 facilities. The grounding follows on the heels of a major Microsoft outage that has affected many Microsoft-hosted services, particularly email, for more than 24 hours so far. There's no indication presently that the two incidents are related. We'll update this story as more information becomes available.® Updated to add at 2353 UTC CBS News reports that “an update to the private communications network that connects America’s air traffic control system caused the system to reboot. When the FAA’s telecommunication infrastructure rebooted, it crashed, causing the communications outage. The system is operated by L3Harris.” L3Harris has not responded to a request for comment. Updated to add at 2340 UTC Air Space Intelligence (ASI), awarded the FAA’s $875 million, 12-year contract for its new Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system, has issued a statement asserting that its products played no role in the FAA’s flight suspension. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said.

articles.title: Blue Origin puts its space station plans on hold to concentrate on moon missions instead
articles.content: Artwork shows an early conception for the Orbital Reef space station, a project led by Blue Origin. (Blue Origin Media) Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin space venture has decided not to seek further NASA funding for its Orbital Reef space station project in order to tighten its focus on lunar missions. For the past five years, Blue Origin has played a lead role in Orbital Reef , alongside partners including Sierra Space and Boeing. In late 2021, Blue Origin won a $130 million contract from NASA in the first phase of the space agency’s Commercial Low Earth Orbit Destinations program, or CLD. Now NASA is seeking proposals for the next phase of the program , which will fund the development of orbital outposts to replace International Space Station in the 2030s. Proposals are due on Dec. 8, with contracts expected to be awarded next spring. Blue Origin indicated that it will not submit a bid. “Blue Origin’s mission is to build a road to space for the benefit of Earth so that millions of people can live and work in space. Establishing a sustained human presence on the moon is a critical step toward that future,” the company said in an emailed statement. “As our role supporting NASA’s Artemis and Moon Base missions continues to grow, we’re focusing resources on capabilities that directly advance our lunar projects,” Blue Origin said. “By sharpening that focus, we can move faster on the technologies and infrastructure needed to make lunar permanence a reality.” Orbital Reef was once touted as a “mixed-use business park” in space — and was even slated to star in a sci-fi thriller titled “Helios.” But much like that delayed film project, the space station is now on the back burner. Orbital Reef isn’t the only initiative Blue Origin has put on hold to prioritize moon missions. In January, the company suspended its suborbital New Shepard program for at least two years for similar reasons. Blue Origin is building landers for delivering cargo and crews to the lunar surface for NASA. An uncrewed Blue Moon Mark 1 lunar lander is scheduled for launch early next year, and a crew-capable Mark 2 version is scheduled for testing in low Earth orbit next year during NASA’s Artemis 3 mission. Last week , NASA awarded Blue Origin a $94 million base contract, plus a $140 million option, to deliver a nuclear-powered rover to the lunar south pole. Blue Origin also won a spot in NASA’s broader lunar cargo delivery program. In addition, Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin subsidiary, will contribute to a lunar power-generating project known as miniCAST. Blue Origin is pursuing several other moon development initiatives, including a program called Blue Alchemist that aims to use lunar materials to manufacture solar cells and electrical wire. Several competitors are still working on commercial space stations. Voyager Technologies, Airbus and Northrop Grumman lead the Starlab consortium, which received CLD Phase 1 funding from NASA and is expected to put in a proposal for Phase 2. Axiom Space and Vast are also developing outposts that could take the place of the ISS. Meanwhile, Marysville, Wash.-based Gravitics is building space station hardware for Axiom and an orbital carrier for the U.S. Space Force .
articles.author: Alan Boyle

articles.title: Route coding agent requests to the right model on Amazon Bedrock with NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard
articles.content: Coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex CLI work in tasks. A developer asks for a change, and the agent reads files, edits code, and runs tests until the work is done. One task can take a few model calls or dozens. What the developer pays for is the task, not one call. The price per token alone doesn’t tell you what a whole task costs. The total depends on how many turns a model needs, how much history each turn replays, and how often a task has to be retried or never finishes. You pay for every attempt, including attempts on tasks that never finish. So when you route a coding agent’s requests between models, judge the routing by cost per solved task: the total cost of your runs divided by the number of runs whose tests pass. NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard is an open source library that helps an AI agent choose which model handles each request. You define the models that it can use and the strategy that it follows. Its LiteLLM integration supports two strategies. Stage routing reads the recent tool activity and results in the request history, and then picks one of two candidate models. Random routing picks from the configured models, with optional weights, for traffic splits and A/B comparisons. Another option you can explore is LiteLLM, who also recently shipped a native built-in Switchyard stage router as an auto-router strategy. In this post, you use the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to deploy LiteLLM, an open source gateway for large language models (LLMs), with the Switchyard routing plugin in your AWS account. LiteLLM calls the models on Amazon Bedrock . You then use the sample’s benchmark runners to measure cost per solved task for a routed model group and for single-model baseline groups, so that you can evaluate routing against your own workloads. Note: The sample installs switchyard-server 0.3.0 from crates.io and runs the published LiteLLM v1.102.0 image. NVIDIA documents switchyard-server 0.3.0 as a demo and evaluation component, and its configuration can change between releases. This sample uses the experimental Switchyard LiteLLM integration and its configuration and APIs may change between releases. This is sample code, for non-production usage. Work with your security and legal teams to meet your organizational security, regulatory, and compliance requirements before deployment. Deploy the sample in a non-production account and test it before relying on it. Solution overview Figure 1 shows the architecture of the solution. LiteLLM and the Switchyard plugin run in one container image on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate , in private subnets. Figure 1: Solution architecture A request flows through these steps. The numbers match the diagram. The coding agent sends an OpenAI-compatible request with the model field set to switchyard , the LiteLLM model group that Switchyard routes, and the shared gateway key in the Authorization header. The endpoint is your hostname over HTTPS, with an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate on the load balancer, and only the IPv4 CIDR range that you allow can reach it. With a hosted zone in Amazon Route 53 , Route 53 resolves the hostname to the load balancer. AWS WAF filters the request with IP reputation, known bad input, and per-IP rate-limit rules. The Application Load Balancer forwards only /v1/chat/completions , /v1/models , and /health/liveliness to the ECS task in a private subnet, and answers every other path with 404. The task runs one container: LiteLLM with the embedded Switchyard plugin. LiteLLM validates the gateway key and calls the plugin to pick a model. Stage chooses between a capable model and a lower-cost efficient model. It reads the tool activity and results in the request history, so the agent must send the full conversation history. Random chooses from a weighted pool. Neither strategy calls a judge model. LiteLLM calls the selected model through the Amazon Bedrock Converse or ConverseStream API, with the task’s AWS…

articles.title: I Put a 42-Desk Design Studio Inside My Coding Agent
articles.content: The part after the first design. In October, I pointed Desk Studio at its own launch card. Three roughs, one pick, three polish rounds, scored 8.4, then 8.5, then 8.9, signed off at 8.9 for $1.34 at list price. And I could see every one of those steps while it happened, which is the whole reason the tool exists. Before it, a follow-up like "make the headline bigger" would come back from my coding agent as a whole new design. New layout, new colors, sometimes new copy. Was the headline fixed? Couldn't tell, cause everything else moved too. So Desk Studio splits the job up like a small studio. Rough options first, then one gets picked with notes, a cheaper desk polishes it, a script checks the real pixels, and a senior desk signs it off or sends it back. I still use it on my own projects. What it is. There are 42 desks. The Design Manager runs in your own session and hands out work. The other 41 run as subagents, things like a Typographer, an Art Director, a UI Designer, or an Email Designer. Each one is just a markdown brief in the repo, so if you want to know how the Art Director decides, you open agents/art-director.md and read it. They're grouped into three tiers, and each tier is on a model that suits what it does. Tier Default model What it does Directors (3 desks) Opus the pick, the notes, the sign-off Seniors (17 desks) Sonnet the roughs, research, type, tokens, copy Builders (21 desks) Haiku every polish round, the making It all runs locally. The desks reach models through whatever CLI you're already logged into, claude , codex or agy , or an API key if you'd rather. Apart from those model calls and a few web lookups from the research desks, nothing leaves your machine. In Claude Code it's a plugin. For Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Copilot, Windsurf or OpenCode it's one line in the project: # Claude Code /plugin install desk --marketplace adityareddy-dev/deskstudio # Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Copilot, Windsurf, OpenCode npx deskstudio add Then you just ask like you normally would: /desk:design a launch card for LinkedIn # or run the job yourself from a terminal npx --package deskstudio desk-run design "a launch card for LinkedIn" The files land in .desk/out/<job>/ with a short note on who did what, the scores and the cost. How a job runs. Every visual job takes the same path. Roughs. The UI Designer makes three different directions on the senior model, from the brief, your brand file and the standard for that kind of piece. Pick. The Art Director looks at the renders, picks one (or mixes two) and writes notes. Polish. A builder desk works from those notes plus a screenshot of the current render. Rounds are cheap, so this is where the back and forth happens. Proof. A script renders the file in Chrome at every size and checks the pixels. No model. Sign-off. The Creative Director scores eight axes: hierarchy, typography, spacing, colour, composition, originality, brand fit and copy. To pass, every axis needs 8 or more and the average needs 8.5. Fail-proof, and it goes back to the builder with the screenshot. A builder that misses the same note twice hands the file up to a senior, and a senior that misses twice gets one round with the Art Director. After the round cap, the job comes back marked under the bar, with a note on which axis fell short, so it won't quietly ship something that didn't pass. Here's a real terminal run of exactly that, on OpenAI models this time. Proof caught a type-scale problem in round 2, the builder fixed it, and round 3 still came back under the bar cause originality only got a 6. The last lines say what's missing. Splitting out the pick was deliberate. Once a direction is picked, every round after that is a fix to that one design, so a note like "type sizes, not layout" means the next round touches type sizes and nothing else. When every round is a fresh design, there's nothing steady to measure against, which was the whole problem in the first place. Proof has no model in it for a similar…

articles.title: Match Group Keeping AI Out of Dating
articles.content: Match Group is embracing artificial intelligence across its business, but CEO Spencer Rascoff says AI agents won't be allowed to date for users on Tinder, Hinge and its other apps. Rascoff says Match wants its platforms to remain a “human-only zone,” even as the company uses AI to verify identities, improve safety and block harmful messages. He joins Bloomberg Businessweek Daily to discuss where companies should draw the line on AI and how the technology is transforming Match Group. He also weighs ibn on Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia and why he thinks companies are ultimately bigger than any one CEO. (Source: Bloomberg)

articles.title: CI Failure Triage Needs Evidence Before It Needs a Classifier
articles.content: If you have ever owned a CI pipeline and cleared a wall of red builds before standup, you might recognize this routine. A nightly run finishes with thirty-seven failed tests, and by the time anyone looks, thirty have passed on a rerun and picked up a flaky tag while the other seven get tickets. Nobody records why the thirty failed in the first place, so the same failures come back the next night under the same label. And it is easy to see why teams settle into this, because a rerun clears the build in minutes while finding the real cause of thirty failures could take the whole team a day. That gap is where a new class of AI models starts to look tempting. Shawn Gordon’s recent HackerNoon explainer introduces Jev , a decision model from TypeSafe AI that writes nothing and only picks an answer. It chooses from up to 255 options or returns a yes or no probability in about half a second. TypeSafe also says those probabilities are calibrated, so an answer given at 80 percent confidence should be right about 80 percent of the time. Sorting a failed test into a product defect, environment noise, or an agent error is a three-option choice question, which makes it look like a natural fit. But when Mastra, the company behind an open-source framework for building AI agents in TypeScript, tested Jev on a related triage job, the results were poor. Jev labeled 78 of Mastra’s own GitHub issues as urgent, high, or low, using only each issue’s title and body, and only about 10 of its answers matched an engineer’s judgment. Mastra concluded that the model could not see the evidence that priority depends on, and Gordon put the risk plainly in his explainer. “A consistently wrong classifier that runs cheaply is just a faster way to tag things badly.” CI triage has the same trap, because a model can sort failures well only when the pipeline has kept the evidence that separates one category from another. So the evidence has to come first and the classifier second . Three Failure Categories Need Three Different Owners Most pipelines record a failed test as one status, and that single status hides three kinds of failure that need different fixes from different teams. Sai Krishna , Director of Engineering at TestMu AI (formerly LambdaTest), draws that line before any fix starts. “We should ideally treat these failures into three different categories,” he explains. “Whether it is a product defect, like an actual defect in the product. Or if it is environmental noise, maybe a network issue, a latency problem, a backend API that went down. Or very importantly now, since agentic pipelines are involved, whether it is an agent error.” He also gives a working definition for the third category, which is the one teams find hardest to name. “If the agent’s reasoning or actions are inconsistent, that is the point where we can clearly say it is an agent error,” Krishna says. “We have to put them in different buckets.” Each bucket leaves a different trail, and that trail is what a classifier will eventually read. A product defect reproduces on the same commit under the same conditions and usually traces back to a recent change in the application. Environment noise shows up as timeouts or 5xx responses from a dependency, and it tends to hit unrelated tests in the same time window. An agent error happens in a healthy environment and with an unchanged commit, while the agent’s steps differ from the last passing run. So the first practical move is to write those signals down as rules for each bucket and to name an owner for each one. The feature team takes defects, the platform team takes noise, and whoever owns the prompt and the model takes agent errors. Parallel Runs Hide a Fourth Category Inside the Noise Three buckets cover most failures, but some failures look like environment noise only because of how the suite runs. Srinivasan Sekar , also Director of Engineering at TestMu AI , sees this most often when teams move from local runs to large parallel grids. “The…

articles.title: HomeView Tidbits: Mirror, Sleep Timer, and Other Details
articles.content: Apple's HomeView is out today, and we're finally learning all the little details about the new hub. We've rounded up a list of tidbits for those setting up a HomeView or thinking about getting one. Sunglasses Apple says the HomeView probably won't recognize you if you have your face covered, including when wearing sunglasses. If HomeView isn't identifying you, Apple suggests removing anything that would block the camera from seeing your face. The HomeView's screen needs to be angled toward your face, you need to be centered in the frame and closest to the camera if other people are around, and the HomeView can't be blocked by overhanging shelves and cabinets. Apple says the HomeView needs front-facing, even light. Mirror There's a "Mirror" in the HomeView Control Center that lets you use the camera to see yourself. There's an option to turn on an edge light for face illumination, along with 1x and 2x zoom. Guest Controls The HomeView owner has multiple options for what guests can access. Safari can be turned on or off, or adult websites can be blocked. By default, guests can use Siri for general knowledge, writing help, and math help, but ‌Siri‌ features can be turned off. Explicit content can be turned on or off. There's an option to choose which Apple Music subscription supplies music for an unrecognized user. Wi-Fi/Cellular The HomeView authenticates people through face recognition and by making sure their iOS device is nearby, recently unlocked, and on the same Wi-Fi network as the HomeView. If there's a Wi-Fi outage, Apple says cellular can also be used to unlock personal content as long as it's in the same location and was recently on the Wi-Fi network. Sleep Timer You can set a sleep timer on HomeView to pause whatever media is playing when the timer goes off. No Buttons There is no button to turn the HomeView on or off, or restart it. It can be restarted from the Settings app or by briefly unplugging it. Logins You can log into websites and apps using your iPhone, similar to how the Apple TV works. Notifications The HomeView only has notifications for phone calls and home devices, with an option to toggle on critical notifications. There are no other notification settings or options. Liquid Glass The transparency of the Liquid Glass interface can be adjusted from clear to opaque like on iPhone, iPad , and Mac. Personal Data Lockouts If someone tries to repeatedly access personal content on HomeView that needs authentication, facial recognition via the camera is disabled and you'll need to prove identity with a registered device. Related Roundup: Apple HomeView Buyer's Guide: HomeView (Buy Now) Related Forum: HomePod, HomeView, CarPlay – Home & Auto Tech This article, " HomeView Tidbits: Mirror, Sleep Timer, and Other Details " first appeared on MacRumors.com Discuss this article in our forums

articles.title: Architecture patterns for fast session startup on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime
articles.content: Agents today review code, process claims, and run unattended for hours. Many also sit behind interactive experiences where a person waits for the first response. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime gives these agents a fully managed, serverless environment: each session runs in its own isolated microVM, the platform scales to zero when there’s no work, and you only pay for the resources your sessions consume. AgentCore runtime with platformVersion set to “V2” changes how sessions start. Instead of initializing your container for every session, it prepares your environment once, snapshots it, and restores that snapshot for each new session. Session start times are faster and more consistent. V2 also reclaims memory your sessions don’t use, so your bill tracks what your agent uses. For most agents, switching to V2 is all it takes. Some agents need restructuring to get the full benefit, and for chat and voice experiences even 2 seconds is too slow. This post explains how V2 starts a session, how to measure session start time, and how to keep work off the first request, including build hooks, which AgentCore runtime now supports. We cover four patterns, from changes to your agent’s code to starting sessions before users need them. Which pattern do you need? Your situation What to do Section A new session in about 2 seconds is fine Switch to V2 and do all initialization before app.run() Keep work off the first request Your agent needs large files, a CLI, or a browser early, and can’t hold them in its process Add a build hook to load and prime them while the snapshot is built Working with hooks You need sub-second, and users engage before they send their first request (opening the app or a chat window) Start the session in the background when the user engages Pre-warm on user engagement How V2 starts a session AgentCore runtime runs each session in a new microVM. On V1, AgentCore pulls your container image from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), starts the container, and runs your initialization code before it can process the first request. The image pull dominates, so cold start grows with image size. V2 does that work once. When you create or update a runtime, AgentCore runtime starts your container in a fresh microVM and waits for the first healthy ping ( GET /ping ), which must arrive within 120 seconds. It then clears the operating system’s file cache, to keep the snapshot small, freezes the microVM, and stores its memory and disk as a snapshot. This is a change from V1: Every create or update now takes a few minutes while the snapshot is built. In this post, init means everything your agent does before /ping reports healthy. With the AgentCore Python SDK, that’s everything before app.run() . If you run your own HTTP server, in Node.js or another language, report healthy only after your initialization finishes. Figure 1: Build, once per create or update When a new session arrives, AgentCore restores the snapshot into a new microVM. Your process resumes exactly where it was frozen, with its imports, objects, and clients in place. Files from your image are loaded lazily: each block is fetched the first time a session reads it. Figure 2: Invoke, every new session Three facts follow from these flows, and the rest of this post builds on them: Memory comes back whole. Anything your process held at snapshot time, and anything in a RAM-backed file system such as /dev/shm , is available at memory speed from the first access. File reads don’t carry over. The file cache is cleared before the freeze, so reading a file during init doesn’t make it fast in a restored session. Image files are fetched on first read. The first read of a block comes from snapshot storage and is then cached closer to the host. articles.title: Millions of Americans are not taking their GLP-1 drugs as prescribed
articles.content: GLP-1 medications are everywhere these days. The peptide-based drugs are both highly effective and wildly popular for diabetes, weight loss and a growing range of connected chronic health conditions, including cardiovascular disease and obstructive sleep apnea. But, amid the boom, the latest data suggests millions of Americans have turned to unapproved versions and are using the potent drugs in ways doctors never intended, raising questions about what that real-world use means for safety and efficacy. In a study published this week , researchers at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention broke down survey data of GLP-1 use collected between July and August of 2025. Based on responses from over 8,000 US adults, the researchers estimate that about one in 10 US adults (9.8 percent) used a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, aka GLP-1 medication, in 2025. That's around 27 million adults. The study was published in the CDC's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. Among GLP-1 users, nearly half (44 percent) reported using their GLP-1 in a way that was different from how it was prescribed. Users skipped doses, delayed getting refills, and used smaller doses than prescribed, among other changes. More than half of the people modifying how they used the drug said the changes were because of cost or availability reasons. Cost and access barriers were most pronounced among younger GLP-1 users. Fifty-eight percent of adults 14­–39 years old who modified their use cited cost as a barrier, compared with just 20 percent of adults 65 or older who said the same. Read full article Comments

articles.title: OpenFold3 on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart: Predict biomolecular structures
articles.content: You can deploy OpenFold3-preview from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart . The OpenFold Consortium and the AlQuraishi Lab at Columbia University developed OpenFold3 as an open source biomolecular structure prediction model. With a few lines of code, you can typically deploy OpenFold3 into your own AWS account. You can then predict the 3D structures of proteins, DNA, RNA, small-molecule ligands, and the complexes they form. The endpoint runs with network isolation, which you can use to help keep your sequences within your AWS account. Computational drug discovery teams now use structure prediction as a core part of their work. Teams use it in target identification, antibody and protein engineering, and structure-based virtual screening. Teams have found running these models challenging. You need GPU infrastructure, a working CUDA and PyTorch stack, large model checkpoints, and a serving layer that handles requests that take minutes rather than milliseconds. SageMaker JumpStart can handle much of that work for you. OpenFold3 runs in an AWS-maintained container on a managed Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint. The endpoint is designed to handle request queuing and GPU warmup, and you can add autoscaling. In this post, we show you how to: Deploy OpenFold3-preview on a SageMaker asynchronous inference endpoint. Submit structure prediction jobs and interpret the results, including predicted structures and confidence scores. Run several predictions in parallel on multi-GPU instances . Supply your own multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) to improve prediction accuracy while helping keep your sequences private. Help reduce costs by scaling your endpoint to zero when it’s idle. Overview of OpenFold3 OpenFold3 is an all-atom structure prediction model. It predicts the joint 3D structure of a set of molecules from their sequences. It isn’t limited to single protein chains: It can fold multi-chain protein complexes, protein–nucleic acid assemblies, and protein–ligand complexes in one prediction. Attribute Details Developer OpenFold Consortium / AlQuraishi Lab, Columbia University Model type All-atom biomolecular structure prediction Inputs Protein, DNA, and RNA sequences. Small-molecule ligands as SMILES Outputs Predicted structures in mmCIF format, with confidence metrics (pLDDT, PAE, PDE) Version OpenFold3 0.4.1, of3-p2-155k checkpoint License Apache 2.0 JumpStart model ID huggingface-proteinfolding-openfold3 Supported instances ml.g6.2xlarge , ml.g6.4xlarge (default), ml.g6.12xlarge The OpenFold3 developers release its code and model weights under the Apache 2.0 license, and they publish the training data and methods. Research organizations and pharmaceutical companies can inspect the model, fine-tune it, and build on it under the terms of that license. The developers describe OpenFold3-preview as a research preview. Use cases Target and complex structure prediction – Predict structures for targets that have no experimental structure, including multi-chain assemblies and protein–nucleic acid complexes. Protein–ligand co-folding – Fold a protein together with a small molecule supplied as SMILES to generate binding-pose hypotheses for structure-based design. Antibody and protein engineering – Evaluate designed variants by predicting their structures and comparing confidence across candidates. High-throughput screening pipelines – Queue large batches of prediction jobs against an autoscaling endpoint and process the results directly from Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). Why OpenFold3 uses asynchronous inference Most JumpStart models, such as large language models and embedding models, deploy to real-time endpoints. A real-time endpoint returns its response within a single request, and that request is capped at 60 seconds. Structure prediction works differently. Folding time grows with the number and length of the chains in a query, and real-world proteins and complexes often take several minutes. For this reason, OpenFold3 on JumpStart runs on…

articles.title: 3 best new to Netflix movies you should stream this weekend — including a new mystery thriller set in Music City that stars an Oscar winner (Nov. 13–15)
articles.content: With all of the new titles regularly popping up on Netflix each month, it can be hard to narrow down exactly what you want to watch once you've plopped yourself on the couch and picked up the old remote. And the streamer's November 2026 slate has been no exception, with 51 fresh flicks added to the already extensive platform this month alone. But with yet another weekend upon us, we at Tom's Guide thought we'd make things easier for you and curate an easy, breezy list of three movies that are well worth your time and attention. If you're a horror-movie fan , you'll be happy to hear that the freaky 2022 hit " Smile " is back on the streaming service. For action lovers, there's the new Indonesian survival thriller, but if country music and Jessica Chastain dramas are more your vibe, the streamer's new Nashville-set mystery original might be up your alley. That's enough to keep you busy until Monday, surely. Here are three new-to-Netflix movies to add to your weekend watchlist. 'Heartland' (2026) Jessica Chastain has famously played a country star before — she received both Emmy and Golden Globe nods for her work as the heavily hair-sprayed crooner Tammy Wynette in "George & Tammy" — but " Heartland " pulls that musical beat into the mystery genre. In this Nashville-set noir written and directed by Shana Feste ("Country Strong", "The Greatest"), the Oscar winner plays former country singer Misty Jones, who comes out of retirement to investigate the disappearance of her niece (Carter Faith), who is also a rising country performer. Misty's search forces her to grapple not only with Nashville's seedy underbelly but also the demons of her own past. Garrett Hedlund, Carter Faith, Ross Lynch, Paul Sparks, Jennifer Nettles and John Hawkes also star. Watch "Heartland" on Netflix now 'Never Surrender' (2026) When a gang of ruthless criminals descends on a small remote village in Central Java, guilt-ridden grandfather Eyang Hari (Lukman Sardi) becomes an unlikely hero, tapping into his past as a former special forces soldier to save the lives of his two estranged grandchildren, Putri (Callista Arum) and Dimas (Sultan Hamonangan). Directed by Sidharta Tata, the action film “balances high-stakes combat with a heartfelt story about family,” says Netflix, “highlighting the emotional journey of three generations as they rebuild trust amid grief and atone for the past.” Watch "Never Surrender" on Netflix now 'Smile' (2022) After witnessing a brutal and bizarre incident involving a patient, Dr. Rose Cotter’s (Sosie Bacon) life begins to unravel, with terrifying visions and disturbing occurrences disrupting her days. Those increasingly sinister and supernatural events all seem tied to a malevolent entity that feeds on trauma and passes from victim to witness, each marked by an unsettling fixed grin. To break the deadly curse before it destroys her, Rose turns to an old flame (Kyle Gallner) for help and must confront her troubled past to escape her horrifying new reality. Written and directed by Parker Finn in his feature directorial debut, “Smile” was an absolute horror hit, grossing $217.40 million worldwide and winning over critics. With an 80% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes , the site’s critical consensus praised: "Deeply creepy visuals and a standout Sosie Bacon further elevate Smile 's unsettling exploration of trauma, adding up to the rare feature that satisfyingly expands on a short." articles.title: Anthropic now lets you self-host Claude Managed Agents. The catch? 8 hours to act if it flags a safety risk
articles.content: Anthropic has unveiled a self-hosted version of its platform for building and running AI agents. Self-hosted Claude Managed Agents , as it’s aptly called, is available now in private beta. Customers host both the server that coordinates the agents and the sandboxes where the agents run their tools, either in their own cloud account or in an on-premises data center. Credentials and session histories stay on their infrastructure, while requests to Claude go to the inference provider they configure. While the benefits of self-hosting are evident, particularly for companies handling sensitive data, the accompanying license comes with a number of notable caveats that may give some customers pause — this includes strict deadlines for responding to safety notices, limits on which models customers can use, and rules against preventing certain types of data from being sent to Anthropic. Claude’s road to self-hosting Back in April, Anthropic debuted Claude Managed Agents , a hosted service for building and running AI agents. The following month, the company launched self-hosted sandboxes , which let customers run agents’ tools on their own infrastructure while Anthropic continued to run the Claude Managed Agents server. With self-hosted Claude Managed Agents now in the mix, customers can run that server themselves, too, and store session histories in their own database. In a blog post marking the launch, Anthropic says agents are taking on more consequential engineering tasks, including repairing failed builds, checking releases and deciding which alerts need attention. That work can require access to sensitive systems, such as private code repositories and internal build and release systems. “For agents with that level of access, some teams want the whole service in their own environment, not just the sandbox.” “They run unattended on your code and need access to your internal systems,” the company writes. “For agents with that level of access, some teams want the whole service in their own environment, not just the sandbox. Until now, that meant building the platform themselves.” Several companies have done exactly that. Spotify developed Honk , which runs Claude through the Agent SDK inside Spotify’s own harness. The company deploys Honk in Kubernetes pods in its cloud environment, giving it access to its internal CI systems so it can run builds and verify its code changes. Anthropic’s new offering packages much of that work into a product. Customers run Anthropic’s server and the sandbox workers in their own cloud or data centre, with PostgreSQL if they want to retain session histories across restarts, while their developers use the same core APIs as they do with the hosted service. The local server can send requests to Claude through Anthropic’s API, a cloud provider such as Amazon Bedrock or Microsoft Foundry, or the company’s own gateway. The devil in the detail: 8 hours to act While Anthropic’s formal announcement emphasizes why companies might want to host the service themselves, digging into the details of the license reveals how much control Anthropic retains over the software once it’s deployed. For starters, Anthropic ships the server as a proprietary binary that customers can’t modify, meaning that they can’t patch or customize the server code themselves. They can route requests through their own gateway, but only to Claude models. The license also bars models from other developers unless Anthropic expressly permits them, and the public inference docs list only Claude models. Among the most notable terms of the license is how little time customers have to act on Anthropic’s safety notices. If the company flags a safety, security or misuse risk in writing, customers have just eight hours to disable the affected feature or roll back the version across every deployment. They also have one business day from…

articles.title: FAA expands AI advice to manage air traffic congestion across entire US airspace
articles.content: The US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system. Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has said it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment. “After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10. articles.title: Google Pixel bug reveals hidden Private Space when switching between light and dark mode
articles.content: TL;DR Google’s November 2026 Pixel update still hasn’t fixed a Private Space bug that first surfaced in September. Switching between light and dark modes causes the hidden Private Space section to reappear in the app drawer, even when it’s set to remain hidden. Google has acknowledged a potentially related issue on its Issue Tracker, but there’s no confirmed fix yet. Google’s big November update packs dozens of bug fixes , but a recent Private Space issue, which unhides the hidden folder in the app drawer, appears to have again slipped through the cracks. For reference, the bug first surfaced following Android 17 QPR1 in September. Fast-forward to Android 17 QPR2 , and the bug is still there. For those unaware, Pixel’s Private Space lets you create a sandbox within your phone. It essentially acts as a separate, locked space where you can keep apps, folders, files, and anything that you want to keep away from prying eyes. The locked space appears at the bottom of the Pixel app drawer, though users also have the option to completely hide the space’s existence.

articles.title: Chinese AI labs are training models on Nvidia's Blackwell despite export controls, says ex-OpenAI engineer
articles.content: US export controls are not stopping AI labs in China from using restricted Nvidia chips, according to a report from a former OpenAI engineer. Will DePue, who left the AI giant earlier this year to launch Unemployment Labs, an AI research consultancy, published forensic evidence showing that "DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group have gained access to Nvidia's Blackwell GPUs, despite restrictions on exporting these chips to China, and are using that hardware to create their AI models." "This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it," said DePue in a social media post . "When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern – a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model." It doesn't sound that insane. The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang followed from revelations that he had an affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who, in 2023, founded Singapore-based Megaspeed International. That company is reportedly under investigation by US authorities for allegedly smuggling Nvidia chips to China. Huang's departure coincides with a renewed push to tighten US chip export controls. House Speaker Mike Johnson supports the idea . And there are at least four bills awaiting consideration that aim to limit China's access to leading edge AI tech: the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act, Match Act, and the Cloud Security Act. On Monday, US Senators Jim Banks (R-Ind.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) cited Jensen Huang's "relationship with a suspected Chinese spy" as a justification for passing the AI Overwatch Act, which would codify the Trump administration's existing chip export controls. The Trump administration on Thursday said it's not sure whether Alice Huang was a spy, an allegation denied by Beijing and currently under investigation by the FBI. Whatever the case, the current rules clearly are not working. Only a few weeks ago, Lava, an Israel-based security company, said it had found "32 Nvidia B300 GPUs, part of Nvidia's Blackwell Ultra generation, through publicly exposed monitoring endpoints with IP addresses geolocated to China." These GPUs, Lava noted, are subject to US export controls [PDF]. The security biz said its findings followed from the exposure of monitoring systems intended for internal infrastructure management that were publicly exposed. How DePue reached his conclusion The analysis published through DePue's consultancy, "Top Chinese Frontier AI Models Carry the Fingerprint of Export-Controlled Nvidia Blackwell GPUs," takes a different approach: analyzing the published weights of various models from Chinese AI labs. As described in the report, model weights – the parameters that change in relation to training data – must be initialized with some value. One method for doing so involves a pseudorandom number generation (PRNG) algorithm called Philox. The algorithm starts with a seed value that produces the same set of initial values whenever it's run. Using PyTorch, initialization can be done by creating multiple GPU threads that work in parallel, with the help of Nvidia's cuRAND library. And because this process is not truly random, it's possible to select a chip and a seed value, generate the initial weights for that hardware and compare that pattern to a model's published weights. "I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models," said DePue. "In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models – including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3 – were initialized on Nvidia Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in Nvidia's flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems." Noting that…

articles.title: Google gets ready to kill off Pixel 10 Magic Cue in favor of Proactive Assistance
articles.content: TL;DR Magic Cue launched on Pixel 10 phones, offering to find useful info in your apps and bring it to your attention. Proactive Assistance debuted with the Pixel 11 series, working quite similarly to Magic Cue, and we’ve been wondering if it’s meant to replace it. New text strings now highlight Google’s plans to move Magic Cue users to Proactive Assistance by the end of 2027. Google first introduced Proactive Assistance with the Pixel 11 series this year, and now it looks like the company is getting ready to fully replace Magic Cue with its new system — eventually. APK teardown: This reporting is based on work-in-progress code. These features may not ship. Magic Cue debuted with Pixel 10 phones, attempting to proactively surface information from apps around your phone when you need it most. But then when we got Proactive Assistance on the Pixel 11 , it largely just felt like more of the same. We even looked at some evidence that seemed to support the idea that Proactive Assistance might be designed as a replacement for Magic Cue .
articles.author: Stephen Schenck

articles.title: Mozilla to Shut Down Solo, Deleting Users' Websites and Data
articles.content: Mozilla is shutting down Solo, its AI-powered website builder and hosting service, on November 30. A notice on the Soloist.ai homepage reads: "We've made the difficult decision to close Solo. We have appreciated all of your support building and growing this product, and the feedback we've received from all of you. Solo will cease operations on Nov 30, 2026." The Register reports: Mozilla launched Solo in December 2023 as a "Mozilla Innovation Project," aimed at helping sole traders to build themselves a webpage for their services. Some 54,000 people used its LLM to build pages, and relied on Mozilla to host them -- complete with custom domain names. Users now have just over two weeks left to find a new home for their pages, although Mozilla says it first notified them on October 1. According to the support FAQ, users can download a ZIP containing an HTML export, contact form and newsletter submissions, and a CSV linking to their images. The images themselves must be downloaded separately. Domains purchased through Solo Domains must also be moved to Name.com, with Mozilla handling the transfer after users create an account and supply its code. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: These 6 AI robot pets might be the cutest gifts of 2026
articles.content: If you've always wanted a pet but don't fancy the responsibilities of feeding, walking, or cleaning up after it, then an AI-powered robot companion might be just what you're looking for this Christmas. From fluffy creatures that develop their own personalities to robot dogs that can recognize your face and desktop companions that actually talk back, AI pets are getting smarter, cuter, and more lifelike all the time. The best part is that there's something for almost every budget, whether you're looking for an affordable little robot to keep you company at your desk or a sophisticated AI pet that can learn from your interactions and develop a personality of its own. I've rounded up 10 of the most interesting AI pets and companions I could find this Christmas, and while they might not replace the real thing, they're certainly a lot easier to house-train. Let's get started! Perfect AI pets Casio Moflin Ai Pet Robot Companion A furry AI pet that reacts to being stroked and develops its own behavior over time. Probably the most emotionally interesting of modern AI pets because Mofflin only reveals its feelings over time as you build up a bond with the little furball. Loona Loona Robot Pet Dog Chatgpt-4o Smart Ai-Powered Companion This AI pet rolls around, recognizes faces, plays games, and supports AI conversations. It has voice and gesture control and an automatic recharge. Loona can see and understand your world through its camera, recognizing faces and gestures. It's a bit like a robot puppy. EMOPET Ai Desk Robot Companion A tiny robot with animated eyes, hundreds of expressions, and a personality that develops through your interactions with it. Thanks to a wide-angle camera, it can see, hear, and understand you. It can explore your desk and even get annoyed with you. Rub it, shake it, and play with it just like a real pet! ropet Ai Robot Pet With 1-Year Chat Memory for Emotional Support & Comfort A fluffy companion that develops one of several personalities depending on how you interact with it. Supports ChatGPT-powered conversations that have a one-year memory. You get 20 minutes of free chat conversations per day, and you can earn extra credits in the app by caring for your pet. ENERGIZE LAB Eilik –your Robot Companion If you want a desktop companion that emphasizes expressive interactions and personality rather than productivity features, try Eilik. Its appeal comes from its animated emotions, playful behaviors, and the ability for multiple Eilik robots to interact, making it a distinctive gift or desk accessory. The original Eilik responds to touch and movement but can't hold AI conversations by itself — you need the separate AI Station to add voice conversations, a camera, and interactive capabilities. TangibleFuture Looi Robot Uses a smartphone as the brains and face of a little desktop robot, with voice interactions and animated behavior. He has his own personality, and his behaviors aren't entirely predictable, which makes him feel truly alive. A lovely example of AI becoming physical. Luka Kids Reading Robot The little owl that reads books to children is designed for ages 6+. The Lula Kids Reading Robot is a camera-based reading robot that recognizes compatible picture books and reads them aloud. More specialized recognition technology than generative AI, so don't expect it to start a conversation. Petoi Programmable Robot Dog Bittle X V2 You can control this miniature robot dog with your voice, app, or via coding because It's a programmable four-legged robot with voice-command capabilities. This is really a STEM Robotics Kit for Kids 10+ & Adults, so it's a gift for someone who loves tinkering with robots rather than simply cuddling them. YONBO Aipi-Lite Ai Companion Robot At the cheaper end of the market is the YONBO Interactive Talking Ai Robot. It's ChatGPT-powered and has Voice Cloning, Memory Storage, and more. This compact interactive companion is based around emotional engagement and playful interactions.
