articles.title: DeepSeek’s coding agent is too tidy for its own good — and benchmarks are punishing it
articles.content: DeepSeek’s open-source coding agent is losing points on a major benchmark for a habit developers usually treat as good practice: cleaning up after itself. The problem surfaced when Hugging Face harness optimization researcher Joël Niklaus added DeepSeek Harness to his coding-agent leaderboard, which compares ten harnesses running the same underlying models. DeepSeek Harness is statistically tied for first across the board’s five scored evaluations, yet on Terminal-Bench alone it drops to sixth, because one built-in behavior caused it to fail tasks that competing agents completed. DeepSeek Harness is statistically tied for first across the board’s five scored evaluations, yet on Terminal-Bench alone it drops to sixth… “One habit explains much of that gap,” Niklaus writes on X , referring to the agent’s weaker Terminal-Bench performance. A tidy habit backfires DeepSeek Harness shuts down background processes when a task finishes, which is a problem for three Terminal-Bench tasks that need those processes to keep running. Niklaus found that DeepSeek Harness passed just two of 36 attempts using DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and GLM-5.3-Flash, while OpenCode, Pi, and Nous Research’s Hermes Agent passed all 36 on those same tasks. DeepSeek Harness passed just two of 36 attempts … while OpenCode, Pi and Nous Research’s Hermes Agent passed all 36 on those same tasks. That behavior knocked between 1.5 and 1.7 percentage points off DeepSeek Harness’s scores. On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at high reasoning effort, it was enough to account for more than the entire 1.3-point gap between DeepSeek Harness and the leader. The leaderboard’s changelog confirms that the shutdown behavior belongs to DeepSeek Harness itself and the results were left unchanged. DeepSeek’s engineering documentation describes its local job registry as a deliberately short-lived component. “Choose it when jobs should live in the harness process and die with it,” it states. Jobs that need to survive restarts or run across processes require a different backend. Same model, different results Niklaus launched his Harness Leaderboard on November 5 after running 28,849 trials across its original nine harnesses using three open models, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash and Flint. He kept the model, provider, and reasoning effort constant while swapping harnesses, and the differences were substantial. Mini-swe-agent, a relatively simple bash-based agent, completed 51.4% of tasks compared with 27.3% for OpenClaw, although several other harnesses were statistically tied with the leader. Costs varied just as dramatically. Pi achieved a 49.4% solve rate at $0.29 per solved task, while OpenCode cost $3.35 per solved task in the initial evaluation. Hugging Face co-founder Thomas Wolf sums up the findings on X as “same open model, different harness => very different results.” The New Stack contacted DeepSeek for comment on the findings but had not received a response by publication time. Orchestration isn’t a guarantee Y Combinator President and CEO Garry Tan has been running separate evaluations using Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol. “ Harnesses differed more on cost than on how often they solved tasks ,” the researchers write. On multi-user tasks, OpenClaw running Opus 5.5 cost roughly twice as much per solved task as the other Opus harnesses, largely because it repeatedly sent context with each request. The project also tested Tan’s gstack workflow skills. In 46 sessions, Opus 5.5 read the instructions but never followed the prescribed steps, and the attempts cost roughly twice as much. The researchers note that the tasks were relatively easy, so it’s unclear whether following the instructions would have improved the results. articles.title: Inside the GPU: A Complete Guide for AI and Machine Learning Engineers
articles.content: A practical technical guide for Machine Learning Engineers, Deep Learning Engineers, AI Architects and GenAI practitioners Introduction: Why every AI engineer needs to understand GPUs Artificial Intelligence has entered an era where computational power is becoming just as important as algorithmic innovation. From training Large Language Models (LLMs) and running transformer architectures to building autonomous AI agents, multimodal systems, diffusion models and real-time inference pipelines, GPUs have become the backbone of modern AI infrastructure. Consider a few familiar activities: Training a neural network on millions of images. Fine-tuning an open-source LLM using LoRA or QLoRA. Generating responses from a 70-billion-parameter language model. Running multiple AI agents simultaneously. Serving thousands of concurrent inference requests. All these workloads depend heavily on how efficiently mathematical operations are executed on hardware. But here is an important distinction: A GPU is not simply a faster CPU. It is a fundamentally different computing architecture designed to execute massive numbers of mathematical operations in parallel. For AI engineers, understanding GPUs means understanding much more than CUDA programming. It means knowing how computation, memory bandwidth, tensor operations, precision, parallelism and hardware architecture interact to determine the performance and cost of an AI system. This article builds that understanding from the ground up. What exactly is a GPU? A Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) is a specialized processor originally designed to accelerate graphics rendering. Rendering a 3D scene involves calculating the color, lighting, texture and position of millions of pixels. Many of these calculations can be performed independently. This makes graphics workloads naturally parallel. Researchers and engineers eventually recognized that the same computational structure appears in machine learning. For example, consider matrix multiplication: This operation is fundamental to neural networks, transformers, attention mechanisms and many other AI algorithms. A CPU can perform these operations efficiently, but a GPU can distribute thousands of smaller computations across its processing units. That makes GPUs particularly effective for workloads involving large-scale parallel mathematical operations. CPU vs GPU: The architectural difference CPU CPU Designed for latency and general-purpose computing. Few powerful cores Complex control logic Large caches Strong sequential performance GPU GPU Designed for throughput and parallel computing. Many processing units Massive parallelism High memory bandwidth Specialized matrix hardware The distinction is not that CPUs are incapable of AI computation. Rather, GPUs are architecturally optimized for the kinds of operations that dominate deep learning. Inside a GPU: Understanding its architecture To understand why GPUs are so effective at AI workloads, we need to look inside the processor. A modern data-center GPU contains several interconnected components: Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs). CUDA cores or equivalent general-purpose processing units. Tensor Cores or specialized matrix-processing units. Registers and shared memory. L1 and L2 caches. High Bandwidth Memory (HBM). Memory controllers and high-speed interconnects. Architecture of a GPU. Credits Let’s understand each component. Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) On NVIDIA GPUs, the Streaming Multiprocessor is one of the fundamental execution units. Think of an SM as a small processing department inside a massive computing factory. Each SM contains: CUDA cores for general arithmetic operations. Tensor Cores for accelerated matrix operations. Registers for fast temporary storage. Shared memory for communication between threads. Scheduling hardware to manage execution. A GPU contains multiple SMs, and each SM executes thousands of lightweight threads over time. For example, NVIDIA’s H100 architecture contains 132…

articles.title: Video Friday: NASA PROMISEs a New Moon Rover
articles.content: Video Friday is your weekly selection of awesome robotics videos, collected by your friends at IEEE Spectrum robotics. We also post a weekly calendar of upcoming robotics events for the next few months. Please send us your events for inclusion. Humanoids 2026 : 6–9 December 2026, SANTA CLARA, CA Enjoy today’s videos! NASA will send a nuclear-powered rover called PROMISE (Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration, depicted in the rendering) to the Moon’s South Pole as a foundational mission in the Moon Base Program. It will be constructed largely from existing hardware—test-bed and flight-spare components—developed for NASA’s ongoing Mars rover missions, Curiosity and Perseverance. [ NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory ] What happens when you put wheels on a humanoid and let a learned controller drive it? We swapped the feet on our Atlas robot to find out; it let us push our actuators, and our models of them, hard. [ Boston Dynamics ] The Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials and Mass-efficient Design (NOM4D) program has achieved the first ever demonstration of automated in-space assembly. A California Institute of Technology (Caltech) payload operating in orbit built a truss structure from individual components. A relatively simple gantry robot (able to move along three linear axes) connected composite truss members using custom-designed joints while simultaneously deploying a thin reflective mesh; a proof-of-concept for future space-based antennas. [ DARPA ] Well, it looks like Amazon’s idea for using mobile robots as security systems is not as dead as we thought it was back in 2020 . [ Amazon Ring ] There are many excellent applications for robots that have a market size of very close to zero, and this is one of them. [ DEEP Robotics ] I don’t know about you, but my philosophy in life is that more tentacles is always better. [ Paper ] Well I’m impressed. [ UZH Robotics and Perception Group ] How Corvus One drones count boxes and read every UPC in case reserve and the singles area at ASICS America’s distribution center. Corvus One flies both areas at the ASICS distribution center in Byhalia, Mississippi, with no localization infrastructure anywhere in the building. No stickers, no beacons, no markers. [ Corvus Robotics ] Thanks, Joan! How do you solve a math problem that might have quadrillions of computations? It’s increasingly a problem for robot fleets in manufacturing and warehouse facilities. Lots of robots, lots of tasks, lots of traffic. Brute force, even with a supercomputer, could take years to find answers. That’s where Toyota Research Institute steps in with a bespoke solver program to elegantly tackle the problem of multi-agent optimal planning. In just one minute, Andrew Best, a scientist at TRI, explains how the company approaches this complex robotics deployment problem. [ Toyota Research Institute ] Rumor has it that printers built by robots never have PC LOAD LETTER errors. [ Flexiv ] Dancing robots are getting even better! Hooray...? [ LimX Dynamics ] It’s season two of AI in Motion, and we’re on a road trip to talk with more of America’s experts in physical AI. We’re rolling into Austin to talk with Jeff Cardenas, who co-founded Apptronik to build robots for humans in very familiar forms. [ Waymo ]

articles.title: OpenAI board member worries an AI "takeover" of society could be months away
articles.content: How do you think you're going to die? If you go by the current statistics for deaths in the US , it's reasonable to expect that cancer or heart disease will eventually get you. But OpenAI Foundation board member and Alignment Research Center Executive Director Paul Cristiano thinks we should all be worried about another major mortality risk. Speaking at a lecture series this week , Cristiano bluntly told the audience in a Toronto Convention Center, "I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident." In the opening lecture of a three-part series , Cristiano outlined his worries about the risk of an impending "AI takeover." He defined that as a situation where goal-pursuing AI systems "call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth" and where any human trying to stop them "would be as ineffective as if you or me was trying to stop the US military." Such a situation would likely lead to mass death and perhaps uninhabitable environments for humans, Cristiano said. Read full article Comments

articles.title: Best AI Video Generation Models in 2026: Elo, Price per Second, Open Weights
articles.content: The AI video leaderboard looks very different from 12 months ago. Native audio is now table stakes. Clips run 15–30 seconds. And an open-weights model sits in the top 3. This ranking (as of Nov 13, 2026) uses one quality signal: blind human-preference Elo from the Artificial Analysis Video Arena . We pair it with API price per second and the license status of the weights. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . Methodology Quality : Artificial Analysis ranks models by Elo from blind pairwise votes by validated evaluators . Each vote compares 2 clips from the same prompt. We rank by the AA-Video-T2V v2.1 (with audio) board. We also report the AA-Video-I2V v2.1 score. Anchor : Kling 3.0 1080p (Pro) is fixed at 1000 Elo on both boards. A score below 1000 means voters preferred Kling 3.0 more often. Price : Artificial Analysis lists cost per minute on each creator’s API. It normalizes to 1080p where offered. We divide by 60 to get price per second. Vendor rates at 720p are often lower, and we flag those gaps. Confidence : Most top-10 scores carry a ±13 to ±15 Elo interval. Models within ~25 points are statistically close. Treat ranks 3–8 as a cluster, not a strict order. Master Comparison Table Rank Model Developer T2V Elo (audio) I2V Elo (audio) $/sec 10-sec clip Open weights 1 Wan 3.0 Alibaba 1175 1108 $0.200 $2.00 No 2 Utopai X Utopai Studios (H3 post-train) 1170 1151 No API — No 3 MiniMax H3 (768p) MiniMax 1161 1133 $0.080 $0.80 Yes (restricted) 4 Dreamina Seedance 2.5 ByteDance Seed 1155 1161 $0.569 $5.69 No 5 Gemini Omni Flash 1.2 Google 1154 1086 $0.104 $1.04 No 6 FLUX 3 Max fal × Black Forest Labs 1153 1068 $0.145 $1.45 No 7 HeyGen Video 1 HeyGen (H3 post-train) 1152 1124 $0.040 $0.40 No 8 MiniMax H3 Max fal (H3 post-train) 1149 1115 $0.160 $1.60 No 9 SkyReels V4 Skywork AI 1137 1125 $0.350 $3.50 No 10 FLUX 3 Black Forest Labs 1137 1071 $0.290 $2.90 No (Dev promised) — Seedance 2.0 ByteDance Seed 1136 1140 $0.374 $3.74 No — P-Video-2-Pro Pruna AI × MiniMax 1130 1116 $0.095 $0.95 No — Pika H3 Flex Pika (H3 post-train) 1124 1114 $0.035 $0.35 Yes (restricted) — Kling 3.0 1080p (Pro) Kuaishou 1000 (anchor) 1000 (anchor) $0.168 $1.68 No — Veo 3.1 Google 964 955 $0.400 $4.00 No — Veo 3.1 Lite Google 948 931 $0.080 $0.80 No — LTX-2.5 Fast Lightricks 943 911 $0.130 $1.30 Yes Source: Artificial Analysis T2V and I2V leaderboards, retrieved November 13, 2026. $/sec = AA per-minute price ÷ 60. “H3 post-train” means the model was fine-tuned from MiniMax H3’s weights. The Rankings 1. Alibaba Wan 3.0: Best overall text-to-video T2V Elo: 1175 (#1) · I2V Elo: 1108 (#11) Price: $0.20/sec at 1080p Weights: Closed Wan 3.0 holds the top text-to-video spot with 7,651 votes behind it. Alibaba launched it on August 24, 2026 . It generates 30-second 1080p clips from text, PDFs and slide decks, priced at $0.20 per second. The document-to-video input is the differentiator. You can hand it a deck and get a structured video back. The trade-off is openness. There are no downloadable weights for Wan 3.0 . Wan 2.2 (July 2025) remains Alibaba’s last open video flagship . Note the I2V gap too: Wan 3.0 drops to 11th on image-to-video. Best for: long single takes, explainer videos from existing documents. 2. Utopai Studios Utopai X: Highest-ranked post-train, no API T2V Elo: 1170 (#2) · I2V Elo: 1151 (#2) Price: No public API Weights: Closed Utopai X is the only model in the top 2 on both boards. Utopai Studios, a Mountain View film studio, built it by post-training MiniMax H3 . It beats the base H3 it came from. Access runs only through Utopai’s PAI platform. PAI charges 93 credits per second , with plans starting at $15 for 1,000 credits. Developers cannot call it from a pipeline. Best for: filmmakers working inside a studio tool. articles.title: Comparing Six AI Video APIs by Cost, Concurrency, and Reliability
articles.content: Most AI video work still starts in a browser tab: type a prompt, wait, download. That breaks down once a team needs 200 product clips a week, a video step inside an app, or an agent that renders drafts overnight. Video APIs move generation into code. In this article, we: how the requests work, a short working example, what matters once real traffic arrives, six APIs side by side, and the automation layer on top. How API Video Generation Works A video takes anywhere from under a minute to a few minutes to render, so no provider keeps an HTTP connection open until the file is ready. Every major video API follows the same three-part pattern. Submit a job. You send a POST request with the model, prompt, and settings. The API answers right away with a request ID and a status URL. Check the status. You poll the status URL, or register a webhook and wait. The job moves from queued to in progress, then to a terminal state such as completed or failed. Fetch the file. The completed response holds a URL to the MP4. Download it to your own storage, because providers delete outputs: Replicate after one hour by default, Higgsfield after at least seven days. The names change from provider to provider. fal calls them requests, Replicate calls them predictions, and Runway calls them tasks. The shape stays the same. Step-by-Step Example: A Text-to-Video Request in Python The example below uses the Higgsfield API and Seedance 2.5. The same submit, poll, and download loop works with any provider. Only the URL, auth header, and field names change. Step 1: Set your credentials. Create an API key in the console and export the key ID and secret. export HF_API_KEY_ID="your-key-id" export HF_API_KEY_SECRET="your-key-secret" Step 2: Submit the job. The idempotency key lets you resend the same request after a timeout without paying twice. import os, time, uuid, requests AUTH = {"Authorization": f"Key {os.environ['HF_API_KEY_ID']}:{os.environ['HF_API_KEY_SECRET']}"} job = requests.post( "https://api.higgsfield.ai/bytedance/seedance-2.5/text-to-video", headers={**AUTH, "Idempotency-Key": str(uuid.uuid4())}, json={ "prompt": "A cinematic tracking shot along a sunlit coastal road", "resolution": "720p", "duration": 5, "aspect_ratio": "16:9", "generate_audio": True, }, timeout=30, ).json() print(job["request_id"], job["status"]) # -> queued Step 3: Poll until the job ends. Four statuses are terminal: completed, failed, nsfw, and canceled. TERMINAL = {"completed", "failed", "nsfw", "canceled"} while True: result = requests.get(job["status_url"], headers=AUTH, timeout=30).json() if result["status"] in TERMINAL: break time.sleep(5) Step 4: Download the video. if result["status"] == "completed": clip = requests.get(result["video"]["url"], timeout=120) with open("clip.mp4", "wb") as f: f.write(clip.content) else: print("Job ended with status:", result["status"], result.get("error")) The official Python SDK (pip install higgsfield-client) wraps steps 2 and 3 into a single subscribe() call. In production, replace the polling loop with a webhook: add an hf_webhook query parameter with your URL-encoded HTTPS endpoint, and Higgsfield sends a POST when the job reaches completed, failed, or nsfw. What Matters in Production Workflows A demo needs one successful call. A production pipeline has to survive timeouts, rate limits, moderation rejections, and bills that grow with every retry. Four areas decide how much work that takes. Queues and Concurrency Every provider caps parallel jobs. Higgsfield allows 20 concurrent requests, fal allows 2 to 40 on self-serve accounts, Runway allows 1 to 20 depending on usage tier, and MiniMax allows 30 in-flight H3 jobs. Put your own job queue in front of the API, such as a database table or a Redis list, so a batch of 500 renders waits its turn instead of failing. articles.title: 5 things Jensen Huang mastered that Nvidia’s next CEO will have to learn
articles.content: The tech world loves superhuman leaders who can withstand boardroom coups and weather negative publicity. Steve Jobs navigated negative press during his tenure at Apple. Elon Musk’s transgressions are forgiven by his followers because of what he brings to his companies. And Sam Altman survived a boardroom coup a little under three years ago. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s one-of-a-kind CEO and figurehead since its founding in 1993, couldn’t survive reports of successive romance scandals. On November 12, he was defenestrated and replaced by his chief financial officer as interim CEO. But in the long term, a permanent replacement will be needed. Finding the right person will be tricky. Huang was renowned for his attention to detail, larger-than-life leadership style, and outgoing personality. He deftly navigated competing business and geopolitical interests to build one of the world’s most valuable companies—and managed to master a wide range of disciplines along the way. So what qualities will his successor have to replicate? Managing geopolitics Huang’s downfall began with a dalliance with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, the CEO of tech company Megaspeed. But one of his biggest strengths was his ability to navigate the messy geopolitics of the AI race between the U.S. and China—and the awkward relationship between Taiwan, home to TSMC, which is central to Nvidia’s chipmaking process, and China, which wants to invade it. “The fact that he was born in Taiwan, is the founder-CEO of Nvidia, and has been able to advocate for less-hawkish approaches to tech policy vis-a-vis China all go hand in hand in giving him perspectives as well as influence within the White House, and a demigod status in Taiwan and Asia,” says Kristy Loke, a researcher at the MATS Program. Loke reckons any future CEO will struggle to replicate that geopolitical deftness. “Instead of Steve Jobs, we’ll get perhaps a Tim Cook,” she says. Handling Donald Trump Game recognizes game, and Donald Trump held Jensen Huang in high esteem. The U.S. president was still defending Huang earlier this week, saying his departure wasn’t necessary. “Between Taiwan and the development of AI in the U.S. and China, Huang has attempted to walk a careful line between the Chinese and U.S. governments, refusing to use adversarial language with respect to China, and uniquely able to attempt to remind political leaders of the major dependence of Nvidia on Asian supply chains and markets,” says Paul Triolo, partner and head of technology for Asia and the Americas at DGA. That could easily have irked the man in the White House. But it didn’t. “He was clearly a staunch supporter of the U.S. leading in the AI race, and frequently only advocated for the sale of GPUs to China several generations behind the cutting edge to ensure the U.S. lead,” says Triolo. “These are policies that both the Biden and Trump administration have supported.” Being a personality and pitchman Nvidia didn’t become one of the world’s most valuable companies by accident, and one of Huang’s strengths was his ability to convince a skeptical public that AI was a technology worth investing in. Like Steve Jobs with his iconic black turtleneck, Huang had his own trademark look—along with the swagger to match—that helped make him one of AI’s most recognizable personalities. One suggestion for his replacement has come from the White House, where Donald Trump has floated Apple’s former CEO, Tim Cook, as a potential candidate to lead Nvidia. That seems unlikely. Schmoozing clients and customers Huang’s downfall stemmed from getting too close to his contacts, but one of his strengths as CEO was his ability to keep people sweet. Taiwanese media regularly covered Huang’s wining and dining of clients, which sometimes involved trips to street food stalls and getting chummy with collaborators. articles.title: The MacRumors Show: HomeView and Apple TV 4K First Impressions
articles.content: On this week's episode of The MacRumors Show , we share first impressions of Apple's new HomeView and Apple TV 4K, including their hardware, everyday usefulness, and experiences with Siri AI. Subscribe to The MacRumors Show YouTube channel for more videos Following a week with the HomeView , Apple's new smart home device makes a strong impression with its build quality and sound, but leaves questions about how much it adds to a household already filled with Apple products. Its overlap with existing devices has already prompted some skepticism. The 7-inch display may feel smaller in person, with its square aspect ratio and thick bezels contributing to an appearance reminiscent of a large Apple Watch. Sound quality from the tabletop model is a highlight, falling between the HomePod mini and full-sized ‌HomePod‌. That also raises questions about the value of the wall-mounted version, which costs the same $299 before mounting accessories but lacks the larger speaker base. In the kitchen, setting timers, playing music, answering questions, and controlling smart home accessories provide straightforward reasons to use the HomeView. Turning web recipes into clean, step-by-step instructions with ingredient checklists is a particularly useful example of where the software is designed around its setting. Elsewhere in the home, its purpose can be less obvious, especially at a desk already surrounded by screens. Review: Is Apple's All-New HomeView Smart Home Hub Worth $299? Personalization is another promising part of the experience. The HomeView's face recognition can switch quickly between household members, bringing up the correct person's apps and information even when two people are standing beside one another. The interface combines familiar elements from Apple's other platforms, but that familiarity also invites questions about whether it feels sufficiently tailored to the home. Messaging and browsing are available, yet typing on a stationary display may be something users do only occasionally. The HomeView has no App Store , instead supporting compatible third-party audio and video apps through a connected iPhone or iPad , just like CarPlay . Video playback offers some flexibility for watching something at a kitchen counter, bedside, or desk, although widescreen content occupies a small portion of the square display. Hands-On With the New Apple TV 4K and Siri AI The fourth-generation Apple TV 4K provides noticeably faster navigation and animations thanks to the A19 chip. Its built-in microphones make hands-free ‌Siri‌ convenient when the remote is missing, including while TV audio is playing. The updated ‌Siri‌ Remote's speaker also makes finding it around the room easier. Support for four-speaker ‌HomePod‌ surround sound provides another reason to consider the new ‌Apple TV‌, particularly for users who already own compatible speakers. We weigh up the appeal of expanding an existing ‌HomePod‌ setup against buying a dedicated home theater system, and consider whether these additions justify the ‌Apple TV‌'s new, higher starting price of $299. ‌Siri‌ AI is a major part of both new products, and its expanded capabilities come with familiar frustrations. More complex questions and requests involving personal context can work, but long waits and inconsistent results can interrupt the experience. Our discussion also touches on occasions when simple tasks, such as adding reminders, prove less reliable than expected, despite the assistant's broader abilities. The MacRumors Show has its own YouTube channel , so make sure you're subscribed to keep up with new episodes and clips. You can also listen to ‌The MacRumors Show‌ on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , Overcast , or other podcast apps. You can also copy our RSS feed directly into your player. If you haven't already listened to the previous episode of The MacRumors Show , catch up to hear our…

articles.title: Forget ‘sponsored’ tags in AI answers. Agent loyalty is what matters
articles.content: No one loves ads, but generally people will tolerate them if it means getting something free or at a lower price. What people won’t forgive? Being lied to. A study looking at how consumers see native ads on news sites—which look similar to editorial content, just with labels—found that fewer than 10% of consumers could identify them as advertising. And when people find out after the fact, they don’t take it well. In a Contently survey , two-thirds of readers said they felt deceived when they realized an article or video was sponsored by a brand. That’s why there’s a whole set of regulations and standards around advertising disclosures that are meant to protect consumers. Now that AI is slowly becoming a central part of our media ecosystem, it’s unclear to what extent those disclosures should carry over into AI answers . After all, if the public is increasingly using AI to shop (47% of U.S. shoppers who use AI started their last product search with AI, according to an impact.com survey , and Meta says shopping is the most common use of its new personal AI agent, Muse ), it feels intuitive that the user should see plainly the commercial interests of the sites that informed any answer. Truth in labeling? A reliable label in AI sounds like a good idea, but it gets complicated quickly. For starters, the label might cause confusion that the AI platform itself was paid rather than the original publisher. In the case of ChatGPT that would potentially conflict with its own ads, which are separate from the answer and labeled as sponsored. OpenAI’s answer to the disclosure question, so far, is the citation link: since launching ChatGPT search , it has included links to sources in answers so users can check them for themselves. All of this gets at the fundamental question of judgment, and which parts of judging a source users have handed over to AI, consciously or unconsciously, simply by using it. When you ask AI to come up with, say, recommendations for air fryers, it’s more like hiring a researcher, not looking at a billboard. In fact, some people turn to AI precisely to get away from the billboards: 24% of the shoppers in the impact.com survey said they use AI to avoid sponsored results and ads. You trust it to hoover up all the information it can find about the question, weigh all the factors—including whether or not any sources are sponsored—and give you the best possible answer. How important is a label at that point? It’d be silly to ask a researcher to stamp every brochure they look at, and pass those brochures over to you in a pile. If AI can solve some of humanity’s most intractable math problems , it can probably reliably weigh the commercial intent of a brand’s FAQ page. In fact, you could argue a label in the answer might cause the reader to over scrutinize an answer the AI has already deemed the most useful possible. AI’s affiliate addiction If we’re considering disclosures, we need to talk about affiliate content, and AI’s outsize reliance on it. As you might imagine, for any query about buying decisions, AI seeks out product recommendations. Those articles are often supported by affiliate revenue, meaning the site gets a fee when the reader takes action, typically a purchase. Legitimate sites that monetize via affiliate disclose that fact on any page with affiliate links; indeed, FTC guidelines require that they do so. However, almost none of those disclosures survive the journey into an AI answer. AI summaries rely heavily on affiliate content: one study found that about a quarter of the pages cited by ChatGPT, Google’s AI Overviews, and Perplexity carried a commercial disclosure, and 86% of answers cited at least one such page. If those disclosures carried over, they’d be in almost every shopping answer. Beyond the UI nightmare that would result, would the label have any meaning at that point? To be clear, no one’s arguing that…

articles.content: When it comes to deciding what to watch, it can get overwhelming sifting through the best streaming services . So I've compiled a TV guide on what to watch tonight. I've gone through everything from Netflix , HBO Max , Apple TV etc to see what's recently landed. I've even added some live sports you can stream on some of the best streaming services, along with movies you can watch for free on Tubi. Here are all the new shows and movies (and live events) you can stream tonight (November 13), and where to watch them. Determined to find her, Misty investigates the people closest to Charlie, uncovering suspicious secrets and confronting uncomfortable parts of her own past. But as the search deepens, she discovers that Nashville's music scene hides a much darker side than she remembers. With dinosaurs and other dangerous creatures roaming their once-familiar streets, the family must stick together, find a way home and fight to survive their bizarre new surroundings. Why you should watch it: "The End of Oak Street" taps into the kind of old-school adventure that made creature features so much fun in the first place. Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor make an entertaining pairing, while the arrival of prehistoric creatures leads to some exciting and genuinely tense encounters. The story unfolds across three timelines: the 12 months of planning, 12 hours of execution and 12 days following the heist. Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan bring an entertaining dynamic to the story, while its three-timeline structure gives the central robbery a few unexpected turns. The series also makes good use of its European locations, with slick action sequences and tense encounters adding to the excitement. It's a solid option for anyone who enjoys a heist movie that keeps you guessing. articles.title: 10 great PC upgrades for under $100
articles.content: The PC hardware scene has taken a real beating during the AI explosion, which means routine upgrades to PCs are drastically more expensive than they used to be. Rather than spending hundreds of dollars on more RAM or a new SSD, why not grab yourself (or a loved one) a cheaper sub-$100 upgrade? As noted, you're probably not going to be able to find a $100 component upgrade to increase your frame rates or jump from 1440p to 4K; at best, you might be able to source yourself a new power supply. So what can you add to a PC for $100? And what makes a good sub-$100 upgrade? Well, the early obvious candidates are improved connectivity, such as a Wi-Fi card or USB-C expansion slots for memory card readers. You could also add a snazzy LCD screen (albeit not Corsair's $250 Xeneon), new RGB fans, or even an AIO cooler. Crucially, just because you're spending less than $100 doesn't mean you have to cheap out on budget or unknown brands. You can still find great quality down at this price bracket from reputable companies like Noctua, TP-Link, and beyond. Here are some of the best PC upgrades you can buy for less than $100. Sm088x 8.8" Universal LCD Screen: $84.99 This Lian Li universal LCD screen can be used either standalone or mounted to a compatible PC case. With vertical or horizontal orientation, its 8.8-inch screen can be used as a USB-powered secondary display for your PC. You can use it to show off PC performance metrics like temperatures, keep an eye on a Twitch stream chat, or control music via your media center of choice. View Deal Peerless Assassin 120 SE: $34.9 Got a dusty old air cooler or a stock cooler that came with your CPU? articles.title: Nvidia Employees Petition For Jensen Huang's Return
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Some Nvidia employees are calling for Jensen Huang's return even after his multiple reported extramarital affairs and abrupt resignation, according to internal correspondence reviewed by WIRED. An internal "suggestion box" post submitted before Huang's resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company's board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to taking any action. The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang. "If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss," wrote one anonymous commenter. "We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance," wrote another. One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang's exit. "I stand by Jensen," the staffer wrote. "Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us." [...] It's been business as usual inside the company throughout this week, but Huang's resignation left many employees stunned. In the hours after, about two dozen employees posted on LinkedIn in support of Huang, with one describing their faith in his leadership as unwavering. Over the same period, WIRED couldn't identify any posts from Nvidia employees in support of his resignation. One employee who has been at Nvidia for a couple of years and wasn't authorized to speak publicly says they perceive the desire for Huang's reinstatement as widespread. They worry the company will eventually suffer without its founder at the helm and say that the board must bring him back. "Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen," the employee tells WIRED. Many employees had expected a board investigation to conclude before any big changes would occur. For instance, the suggestion-box post called on the board to share its findings with employees and formally solicit their sentiment "about Jensen's continuing as our CEO." Instead, Huang left just as the inquiry had begun. Staffers are seeking to better understand why. "If America fails the man who helped build its future," the employee in the companywide email stated, "then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Mozilla leaves Solo website owners to go it alone as hosting shuts down
articles.content: Solo, Mozilla's LLM-powered website builder and hosting service, is shutting down. All sites and data will be deleted on November 30. Mozilla launched Solo in December 2023 as a "Mozilla Innovation Project," aimed at helping sole traders to build themselves a webpage for their services. S ome 54,000 people used its LLM to build pages, and relied on Mozilla to host them – complete with custom domain names. Well, not any more. Now the Soloist.ai homepage says: "We've made the difficult decision to close Solo. We have appreciated all of your support building and growing this product, and the feedback we've received from all of you. Solo will cease operations on Nov 30, 2026." Users now have just over two weeks left to find a new home for their pages, although Mozilla says it first notified them on October 1. According to the support FAQ , users can download a ZIP containing an HTML export, contact form and newsletter submissions, and a CSV linking to their images. The images themselves must be downloaded separately. Domains purchased through Solo Domains must also be moved to Name.com , with Mozilla handling the transfer after users create an account and supply its code. So much for having the fiddly bits taken care of. It also points at a couple of other bot-based site-generating services – in case all this feels like a bit too much. We suspect that for the sort of technophobes that this was aimed at, it very probably will. Mozilla told The Register : "Experimentation is an important part of Mozilla's mission to make the internet better and give people more choice and control online. Sometimes, that means making the decision to bring a product to an end. Solo will officially shut down on November 30, 2026. We initially notified customers on October 1, providing a 60-day transition period, and have been offering support to help them download their website data and migrate their domains purchased via Solo Domains to another hosting provider." It seems that some 54,000 users were not enough to keep it going, and we can see that this would cost money to keep running. An HTML export is a start, though the FAQ doesn't explain how much work it will take to get a complete, functioning site running elsewhere. Buried in the dark recesses of the web is this vulture's own nearly 30-year-old homepage, created using a mixture of Claris Home Page (which was excellent) and Microsoft FrontPage (ever so slightly less so). We saw what a mess machine-generated web content was back then, and thanks to LLMs, we suspect it is almost infinitely worse now. Mozilla might have made a few bucks by finding a commercial partner to take on its users, and perhaps through them offer a paid site-and-domain transfer service. As we noted last year, it seems not to have negotiated anything with KaiOSTech, which maintains and sells what used to be the formerly FOSS FirefoxOS for use on low-end smartphones.

articles.title: Email addresses used in European school bomb hoaxes spotted in old infostealer logs
articles.content: Two email addresses used to send bomb threats that disrupted thousands of Italian schools this week were found exposed in infostealer logs for over a year, experts say. Researchers at Hudson Rock looked into the two university email addresses used to send the bomb threats. One, from Egypt’s Kafrelsheikh University, was scooped up by Vidar – a cybercrime tool that steals saved account credentials and passwords from an infected computer and leaks them to attackers – as far back as October 2021. The other, from Taiwan's Dayeh University, was found among the 284 million addresses included in the massive AlienTXTBASE infostealer dump , dated February 2025. The experts said that the two addresses in infostealer logs do not strictly mean that those behind the bomb threats gained access to the accounts using the previous infostealer compromise. However, it suggests that there was ample time for the universities and Microsoft, which both universities used for authentication, to take action against the accounts that they should have been aware were appearing in infostealer logs. Modern threat intelligence has made infostealer logs highly visible. "Both findings place credential exposure well before the disruption, creating a substantial window in which exposed access could have been investigated and secured," Hudson Rock said . The researchers said that they would need access to details such as the email headers, and data from email providers, including sign-in events and audit records, that could show them more about who sent the email and from what session. Understanding whether the sender authenticated into the account could rule out spoofing, but would not in itself provide proof that the sender used a corresponding password taken from an infostealer log, Hudson Rock noted. There are many ways to get around password-based authentication . The researchers said that in any case where a credential is detected among infostealer logs, the organizations responsible for those accounts must contain them, revoke their access, rotate secrets, and go looking for suspicious activity. "The disruption illustrates why credential exposure deserves attention beyond fraud and data theft," the researchers said. "An account associated with an ordinary university user can become a means of reaching schools, frightening families, and consuming emergency resources." The threats Around 6,300 of Italy's 7,476 state schools received fake bomb threat emails between November 11-12, although only around 390 of them evacuated their respective buildings. The emails contained messaging such as "we will annihilate you," and "we will carry out genocide against Italians," and mention of a "powerful explosive device… with a remote trigger." Early reports suggested that the emails came from a Taiwanese email address and were signed by a "Mikhail Andropov, leader of the Vilayat of Misoginistan" – a fictitious state or region roughly mapping to "the land of Misogyny," with "vilayat" meaning an administrative region of the Ottoman Empire. Various theories have been reported about the identity of the sender, ranging from a teacher based in the Philippines whose email was compromised to a Russia-backed disruption operation. Neither are confirmed. Russia denied any involvement. Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said on Thursday evening that there was no credence to the emails, and that whoever was behind the coordinated hoax sought to invoke chaos across the country. "To date, there is no evidence of a concrete danger," she said, ANSA reported. "These messages aren't intended to shock, they're intended to scare. "Those who write them are primarily seeking our fear, wasted days, suspicion, and chaos. Investigators and the judiciary, along with their European colleagues, are working to determine who is behind them." Schools in France, Ireland, Northern Ireland, and Scotland also received similar emails this week. None of the respective police forces believed the threats…

articles.title: Unannounced Intel Core Ultra 7 260K CPU surfaces in Newegg prebuilt gaming PCs
articles.content: A new Intel Arrow Lake SKU is listed for sale in multiple prebuilt PCs on Newegg, despite no official acknowledgement of the model from Intel. The Core Ultra 7 260K is a downclocked version of the Core Ultra 7 265K from Intel's main Arrow Lake stack, not the Arrow Lake Refresh stack that's infiltrated our list of the best CPUs for gaming . Outside of a few areas on Newegg's website , you'll find no mention of the CPU elsewhere online (including Intel's official Core Ultra Series 2 specs page ). Go deeper with TH Premium: CPU (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Intel VP Robert Hallock sets Nova Lake expectations, teases return to Raptor Lake for DDR4 platforms CPU scaling with DLSS Intel's one-two punch plan in desktop CPUs is taking shape Benchmarking AMD's BC-250, offering Steam Machine-like performance at half the price AMD splits Zen 7 into three EPYC families for 2028 and starts selling server CPUs by the agent Although retailer-exclusive and late-generation variants are common from AMD and Intel — we recently reviewed the Ryzen 5 5500F , for instance — they almost never fly completely under the radar, as is the case with the Core Ultra 7 260K. The chip itself is identical to the Core Ultra 7 265K based on the specs we know, fitted with 20 cores, eight of which are P-cores. The 260K tops out at 5.4 GHz, however, while the 265K reaches 5.5 GHz. Otherwise, the specs are all the same. It comes with the same 125W TDP, same 30 MB of L3 cache, and same support for up to 256 GB of memory running at DDR5-6400. We only know of these specs from an image shown on the two ABS prebuilt listings available with the 260K. It's available in the ABS Kaze II paired with an RTX 5060 , as well as the Flux II Aqua with an RTX 5070 . The image is below, captured hastily, as you can see, from a Microsoft Teams call. Again, we weren't able to find any information from Intel about the chip outside of this slide. (Image credit: Intel) One critical detail this slide confirms is that the Core Ultra 7 260K belongs to the Arrow Lake family, not the range of Arrow Lake Refresh processors like the Core Ultra 7 270K Plus . It tops out at DDR5-6400, while Arrow Lake Refresh climbs up to DDR5-7200. That means the chip doesn't have access to the hardware-level enhancements available in Arrow Lake Refresh, nor the software-based Intel Binary Optimization Tool that boosts performance in select games. Although that's enough to categorize the 260K, there are some details that are unclear. In the two PCs it's available in, the chip is referred to as the 260K across the full product page except in Newegg's option selector (pictured below), where it's referred to as the U7-260KF. Intel's KF models are unlocked for overclocking but lack integrated graphics. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Additionally, the slide from Intel referenced above shows the chip boosting up to 5.4 GHz, but the product page lists the chip at 5.2 GHz for maximum boost clock. Newegg has told us that the chip is exclusive to the retailer and will only be sold through its in-house ABS prebuilts. ABS machines are normally sold with components Newegg already sells piecemeal, offering a convenient way to get a full rig with parts you can identify. The ABS Flux II Aqua, which is available with the chip, is on sale at Newegg now for $300 off. The ABS Flux II Aqua gaming PC comes with an Intel CPU, an Nvidia GeForce GeForce RTX 5070 graphics card, a 1TB NVMe SSD with Gen 4 speeds, and 32GB of DDR5-6000 RAM. This is a 1440p gaming powerhouse with the potential for 4K. View Deal We've reached out to Intel to get more details about the Core Ultra 7 260K, and we'll update this story when we hear back (see update log above). Although the specs suggest the 260K should perform almost identically to the 265K, we haven't had a chance to test the CPU ourselves. And, as you can see from the rankings in our CPU benchmark hierarchy , we recommend most Intel shoppers move toward an Arrow Lake Refresh SKU.
articles.author: Jake Roach

articles.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
articles.content: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. Turning a Windows defense against itself The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates. articles.title: Designing HomeView was a hard but fun journey, says Apple
articles.content: Apple executives have revealed that the new HomeView is the culmination of years of design effort balancing audio, privacy, and especially Siri AI . Designing HomeView was a "hard fought, fun journey," says Apple. As the first buyers take delivery of the new HomeView, two of Apple's executives involved have been discussing the device. Speaking to TechRadar , they describe developing HomeView as a difficult but rewarding journey because of where it is meant to be used. "Home life is super busy, you know, it's complicated, it's complex, and people are moving around," said Matthew Costello , Apple's Vice President of Hardware Engineering, "and we wanted a device that was really designed specifically for that environment." Continue Reading on AppleInsider | Discuss on our Forums

articles.title: Malaysia and Singapore step up Nvidia AI chip probes amidst Jensen Huang controversy
articles.content: Malaysia and Singapore have intensified scrutiny of AI hardware shipments amid concerns about the potential circumvention of U.S. export restrictions on China. Malaysia has launched an investigation into whether AI hardware imported by a subsidiary of the ill-fated Megaspeed was subsequently exported to other countries, reports Reuters . Meanwhile, Singapore has charged another executive over questionable purchases of 917 servers that may contain Nvidia accelerators, according to The Straits Times . The news follows the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang over claims he had multiple extra-marital affairs , including with a possible Chinese intelligence asset who facilitated GPU smuggling into China. Analysts speculate that systematic chip smuggling may be the reason behind his departure . Go deeper with TH Premium: Taiwan, trade, and tariffs (Image credit: tsmc) While the U.S. flip-flops on chip sanctions, China is building its own chip supply market The state of China's decade-long semiconductor push Huawei Ascend NPU roadmap examined China's CXMT targets 30% DRAM memory market share by 2030 with sixth mega-fab China's latest round of rare-earth export controls explained Malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry is examining whether Speedmatrix, the Malaysian subsidiary of Singapore-based Megaspeed , re-exported any of the AI processors and servers it had imported for use in local data centers. Apparently, after months of investigating, authorities have yet to find out whether any such shipments occurred and, if they did, whether they complied with Malaysian laws. Malaysia introduced restrictions on the export, transit, and trans-shipment of advanced U.S.-developed AI accelerators in July 2025, so it now requires companies to obtain appropriate permits. The Malaysian ministry said it was cooperating with customs authorities as well as officials in Singapore and the U.S., and could introduce additional restrictions. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said there was no evidence that Megaspeed-related AI hardware had left Malaysia, but he promised to cooperate with international investigations. Speaking of Megaspeed, the company said on November 12 that it had hired a U.S. law firm to conduct a comprehensive inventory of its AI GPUs and independently assess its compliance with U.S. export-control regulations, reports DigiTimes . The company also confirmed that it had cooperated with inspections by the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) and was prepared to cooperate with other U.S. government agencies if necessary. James Tan Yong Pong, chief executive of Megaspeed, stressed that compliance with U.S. export rules as well as transparent operations were always a priority for the company. However, Megaspeed did not disclose how many GPUs it owns and which GPU models it has, what BIS examined during its inspections, or whether the authorities had identified any violations. Meanwhile, Singaporean authorities have brought 41 criminal charges against Shi Bingzhe, a 34-year-old Chinese citizen who served as director of Superphi and chief operating officer of NJ Global Financial. The two companies purchased 917 servers containing restricted Nvidia hardware from Aperia International in 41 transactions between May 2024 and February 2025, according to prosecutors. Authorities allege that the companies had reason to believe the servers were linked to criminal activity by Aperia International. Superphi now faces six charges, while NJ Global Financial faces 35. The latest charges expand a case that now involves five individuals and six companies. Four firms — Aperia International, A-Speed Infotech, Aperia Cloud Services (II), and Luxuriate Your Life — were charged in July over allegedly making false claims when purchasing servers. Meanwhile, the exact nature of those claims was not disclosed in the report. Authorities have frozen the disposal of a property worth approximately S$55 million and…

articles.title: HPE debuts hybrid storage configs: Rising SSD costs hit supercomputing
articles.content: HPE is pitching high performance compute customers with hybrid configurations of its Cray Supercomputing Storage Systems built for faster throughput, along with a Rack Management Controller that monitors cooling systems. The hardware giant already supplies its Cray Supercomputing Storage Systems E2000 in all-flash, all-disk, tiered and hybrid configurations, but - we're told - the latest combination offers up to 41 percent more data throughput per storage rack. The E2000 line embeds the Lustre open-source parallel file system, and is generally intended to fit NVMe Gen 5 solid-state drive (SSD) building blocks. For the refreshed hybrid configurations, HPE is combining SSDs with new 32 TB SAS-4 (24 Gb/s SAS) HDDs and new enclosures supporting 74 or 100 drives. HPE says it'll deliver up to 116 GB/s of read throughput and 92 GB/s of write throughput per rack, with up to 32 percent more usable storage capacity per rack for expansion to support the growing size of datasets in HPC, especially where sites are mixing AI and traditional simulation-style workloads. One of the reasons behind these new hybrid configurations could be the ballooning cost of storage, caused by the relentless demand for AI infrastructure skewing the price of components such as memory and many other things. But prices for silicon-based NAND flash SSDs are growing faster than those of good old hard drives , as our colleagues at Blocks & Files reported. HPE says that as demand for data-intensive workloads grows, prices for large SSDs have soared. The company claims the new hybrid configurations let research institutions and national laboratories spend less on storage and put that money toward compute node purchases, without giving up on the performance they need. “When making long-term investments in environments where advanced workloads are rapidly evolving, our customers want scalable, dense, and flexible systems to help them address dynamic shifts in requirements," said Trish Damkroger, HPE senior veep for HPC and AI Infrastructure Solutions. The latest hybrid configurations are expected to go on sale in early 2027. HPE's other introduction is a Rack Management Controller, providing what HPE calls "intelligent liquid cooling” via real-time monitoring, leak detection and automated control features. It integrates with HPE Supercomputing Management Software to gather telemetry and provide control. Several platform-specific versions will be offered, each tailored to different rack-scale systems. Support will launch with HPE's own Cray Supercomputing GX5000 infrastructure, naturally, with versions for Nvidia’s NVL72 and AMD’s Helion and Helios kit to follow. The Rack Management Controller will be available for HPE’s kit in March 2027, with support for AMD and Nvidia expected to follow in June. ®

articles.title: Perplexity Releases Decider v1.3: Open-Weight Decision Models Add Locate
articles.content: Perplexity has released pplx-decider-v1.3 and pplx-decider-flash-v1.3 , the latest versions of its open-weight decision models. Perplexity Decider v1.3 is a decision model that returns probabilities, not generated text. It answers yes/no, multiple-choice and score questions about a text or image input. The main addition is Locate, which extracts exact text spans by type or instruction. Weights ship under Apache 2.0 on Hugging Face . Both models also run in the Perplexity Decisions API and on OpenRouter . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Size: 27B on Qwen3.8-27B ; Flash is 4B on Qwen3.5-4B . Hugging Face lists 26B and 5B params. API input: under 256K tokens. Local default: 32,768. Runs on: a CUDA GPU fitting ~49 GiB of BF16 weights (v1.3) or ~8.5 GiB (Flash). No quantized variants. Performance: leads TypeSafe’s Jev 1.14 on most of Perplexity’s self-reported evaluations. Best: 91.6% mean accuracy on 63 query-classification tasks. Worst: Locate averages 69.0, its lowest absolute score. Flash trails Jev 1.14 in finance, programming and law. Bottom line: Best: a 0.27% answer-flip rate and $26.47 per 1M production requests. Worst: every figure is self-reported. What is Perplexity Decider v1.3? Decider is Perplexity’s family of decision models, inspired by TypeSafe’s Jev . Each request has a shared ‘state’ plus one or more questions with labeled options. The model returns a probability per option instead of writing an answer. v1.3 succeeds v1.2 and Flash v1.2 . Flash v1.3 is distilled from the large model. How does Decider v1.3 work? Perplexity adapts a generative LLM backbone into a classifier. The output layer starts from the base model’s LM head, pruned to option tokens (A, B, C). A linear decision head reads the hidden state at a <|marker|> token and outputs option probabilities. Full-attention layers are made bidirectional, which Perplexity’s ablations showed helps. v1.3 also changes attention between questions. In v1.2, every question saw every other question, so answers could shift. In v1.3, the state sees all questions, but each question sees only the state and itself. All questions about one input still run in a single forward pass. Training runs in 3 stages: a full fine-tune on hundreds of public datasets a LoRA specialization adapter a LoRA vision adapter Weights are averaged across 3 seeds. Flash is trained by minimizing KL divergence to the large model’s outputs. What does the new Locate feature do? Locate returns exact text spans with start and end character offsets. Fields can be short labels (‘location’) or instructions (‘Extract the city name where the job is located.’). It targets NER, PII detection and extractive QA. A new <|locate|> token is added per requested field. A span head plus a LoRA adapter is trained, while the backbone and decision head stay frozen. The adapter stays unmerged because merging hurt decision accuracy. How does Decider v1.3 perform on benchmarks? All results below are self-reported by Perplexity : Query classification (63 tasks): 91.6% mean accuracy, 6.54 points above production classifiers. Domain classification: leads Jev 1.14 in all 7 domains, by up to 12.9 points in finance. Retrieval and reranking (72 tasks): 83.99 mean nDCG@10. That is 1.81 above Qwen3-Reranker-8B and 2.24 above Jev 1.14. Multilingual (19 tasks, 8 languages): 88.16% for v1.3, 86.50% for Flash, 85.41% for Jev 1.14. Locate (17 out-of-domain tasks): 69.0 average for v1.3 and 63.6 for Flash. Liquid d1 scores 43.3 and GLiNER large v2.5 scores 33.6. Image classification (5 tasks): 76.99% for v1.3, 1.47 points above Jev 1.14. Flash scores 72.77%. Real-world requests (1M requests, 2,318,887 questions): 93.98% agreement with frontier LLM judges. Jev 1.14 scores 93.35%. Robustness: answer flips on 0.27% of reorder or relabel transformations. Jev 1.14 flips on 2.69% to 4.84%.…

articles.title: Popular gaming chair and desk maker Secretlab launches dedicated US brick-and-mortar locations — new shop in LA, spaces in Best Buy
articles.content: Secretlab, maker of some of the best gaming chairs and also popular for its gaming desks, is launching a brick-and-mortar retail initiative in the US, giving customers the chance to see its hardware in person for the first time. The new stores will open on November 18; the company is opening a dedicated retail store in West Hollywood, LA, as well as dedicated retail spaces at 15 Best Buy locations. Shop the Secretlab Black Friday sale Secretlab Secretlab Secretlab Secretlab Secretlab Secretlab As noted, Secretlab's new stores will open on November 18. Its LA store is located at 8464 Melrose Avenue, West Hollywood, and will feature a physical showcase of its most popular products as well as 1-on-1 consultations. Opening day will feature a luck draw giveaway, with the first 50 visitors entered into a lottery to win a Secretlab Magnus Evo desk. The LA store will include showcases of some of the company's special edition and limited designs, such as its Pokémon collaboration. Beyond LA, the company is launching 15 dedicated retail spaces at Best Buy, in a total of 9 states. Early locations are California, Florida, Colorado, Virginia, Washington, Idaho, Alabama, Pennsylvania, and Texas. The company says more stores are to come. These stores will feature a Secretlab retail setup for hands-on with its chairs and desks. (Image credit: Secretlab) For a product lineup with a heavy physical focus, the opportunity to try out products before you buy should be a welcome one for customers. There will be stock on hand so that customers can take products home with them on the day, rather than having to order online. Secretlab recently unveiled its new Secretlab Atlas , the company's first task chair designed for office work and productivity, rather than gaming. Meanwhile, it still maintains its Titan Evo for games, as well as the Secretlab Magnus Pro and Magnus Evo sit-stand desks.

articles.title: Parents and Teachers Decry Google Pledge To Yank Search If Schools Block AI
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Guardian: Parents and teachers across the US are criticizing Google's announcement that schools choosing to block AI tools could also lose access to Google Search. Google announced last week a range of new AI tools for schools and classrooms, alongside options allowing teachers and administrators to restrict their use. The company said schools should have control over whether students use AI in the classroom, but that schools that choose to block Google's AI tools will also lose access to its search engine. [...] Parents and teachers across the country raised concerns to the Guardian about AI's potential to weaken students' critical-thinking skills and the growing influence of big tech in education. Some called on schools to consider alternative search engines, while others argued that students should be taught how to use AI responsibly rather than prevented from accessing it altogether. Jen Atay, a 51-year-old teacher in Hawaii, lambasted Google's approach, saying: "When the software is free, you are the product, and it is inappropriate for Google to test or develop AI with minors. This should not be allowed at all." A 44-year-old father of two boys in Amissville, Virginia, said he worries that "AI will weaken people's ability to think critically. I use AI in my work, but it would not be effective if I did not have well over a decade of experience under my belt. Even the best models are often flat-out wrong in their responses." [...] Others questioned why schools should depend on Google at all. An 84-year-old retiree and mother in Maryland, said: "Google decided to follow the evil path to riches. When they started, they were great. Today they are simply evil money grubbers Schools should tell Google to go pound sand and simply have kids use DuckDuckGo or one of the other search engines There is nothing Google offers that is not available from some other source." [...] Not everyone believes blocking AI is the answer. Some argued that schools should focus on teaching students how to use the technology responsibly. A 67-year-old emerging technology teacher in Texas said: "I do not blame Google. AI is not going away. I've been very frustrated this year trying to teach AI literacy with AI blocked. Schools need to teach how to properly use AI, not block it." A California resident echoed that view, arguing that schools could use Google's AI tools to teach students to question the information they receive. "Google Search has existed since the 90s and it's crazy of them to completely remove it instead of just removing Gemini. That being said, I would like to see schools actually permit the use of Gemini and use it as an opportunity to show students how its sources aren't always valid and you can't trust everything an AI tells you," they said. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Microsoft outage gives customers a crash course in dependence on Redmond
articles.content: Microsoft 365 services are slowly recovering from a prolonged outage that has handed critics of single-vendor dependence a particularly unwelcome case study. Ever wondered what it would be like if your IT supplier abruptly pulled the plug? Perhaps the result of a mood swing by an unpredictable political leader? For affected Microsoft customers, the disruption has offered an unwelcome preview. Email? Gone. Messaging with Teams? Iffy. Collaboration? Nope. The list of problems in what Microsoft delicately called a "Service Degradation" is breathtaking. The company put the incident's start at 1826 GMT on November 12. Exchange Online fell over. Viewing recently used files in the Microsoft 365 application was problematic. Copilot threw a wobbly. Microsoft 365 Education was affected (unfortunate, considering the changes the company has made ), and so on. At 1401 GMT on November 13, Microsoft reported: "We're continuing to see improvements in service availability," but the damage has surely been done. If the outage halted work at your organization, then questions will have to be asked. Even Microsoft's rivals had some sympathy for the engineers and administrators dealing with the problems. Jos Poortvliet, co-founder of Nextcloud, told The Register : "Mistakes happen in the IT industry. This holds true for companies of all sizes, including us. Our heart goes out to all the admins today. "This incident shows how dependent organizations are on a single ecosystem. Especially in critical infrastructure, monopolies are increasing the risk of stalling businesses globally if an incident occurs. "When everything is hanging on a single vendor, companies can't switch providers quickly to get back up and running, or have a second setup as backup, or pull the plug when under attack and keep working air-gapped." Similarly, Civo CEO Mark Boost noted that IT whoopsies were a way of life. "Every technology provider will experience failures," he said. "The real concern isn't that Microsoft has suffered an outage. It's that we've allowed so much of our critical infrastructure to become concentrated in the hands of so few companies, creating enormous single points of failure." Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons Science and Technology Committee, also commented: "The global Microsoft outage only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the UK's digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services." This week, Microsoft warned users to treat its unsupported Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 as " permanently vulnerable ." Moving to Exchange Online brings its own dependencies, however. Beyond any compensation claims, Microsoft may face awkward conversations about those dependencies when contracts come up for renewal. And there are alternatives. Although perhaps not so extreme as the measures overheard by one vulture in a German shared workspace: "Germany's love of the fax machine – we are finally getting our chance to shine! Our British colleagues cannot email; we have reverted to the natural way of the fax." What a time to be alive. ®
articles.author: Richard Speed

articles.title: Building a Multi-Agent Website Launch Validator With OpenMinion
articles.content: I run a small web agency. We build and host websites for small businesses in the US and Brazil, and every launch has the same floor: a title and a description, a canonical URL, Open Graph tags, JSON-LD, icons, a sitemap, a 404 page that really returns 404, an llms.txt , and a robots.txt that does not lock AI search crawlers out. For years we checked that list by hand, one tab per item. For Cortensor Hackathon 5, I turned the checklist into an agent called Go-Live Gate , built on OpenMinion 0.1, the agent SDK from the Cortensor ecosystem. It answers one question: is this site ready, ready with warnings, or blocked? The code is MIT-licensed at github.com/DesignMaster-Solutions/golive-gate and there is a 2-minute demo at youtu.be/tVH-x62QV3I. This post is about the one design decision that made it trustworthy, and about what it looks like to run an agent on open, swappable inference instead of one vendor's API. The rule: the model never fetches anything The tempting version of this agent is one prompt: "here is a URL, tell me if it is ready". That version hallucinates. It will tell you a sitemap exists because sites usually have one. So Go-Live Gate is split in three agents with different powers: Investigator. It can call three read-only tools: inspect_home , inspect_crawlers and inspect_404 . They are plain urllib with 15-second timeouts and they return facts only (title length, which Open Graph tags exist, which bots robots.txt blocks, the HTTP status of a random missing path). If the model skips a tool, the gap is filled deterministically, so the next step never guesses. Judge. It gets the raw facts and must return a pydantic-validated GoLiveReport : a verdict plus one row per check with the evidence and the fix. The judge has no tools at all. It cannot fetch, so it cannot invent. Publisher. A third agent must call save_report , a tool marked dangerous=True . OpenMinion routes that call through a human approval callback (an interactive y/N, or --auto-approve yes|no for CI). If the human says no, nothing is written. Every run writes facts.json next to report.md . A reviewer can open both and check the model's verdict against what the tools actually saw. That file is the whole point: the agent is only as honest as the layer under it, and that layer has its own offline tests against a local HTTP server. class Check(BaseModel): name: str status: Literal["pass", "warn", "fail"] evidence: str # the fact from a tool result that justifies the status fix: str = "" class GoLiveReport(BaseModel): site: str verdict: Literal["ready", "ready_with_warnings", "blocked"] checks: list[Check] summary: str Why this matters for decentralized inference When the facts live in code and the model only reasons over them, the model becomes replaceable. That is what makes open inference practical for a business tool. OpenMinion talks to any OpenAI-compatible provider. Our recorded runs used a free open-weight model ( nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free through OpenRouter); the same project is set up for the Cortensor Portal with one command ( setup --provider cortensor-portal ). I did not have to rewrite prompts or tools to switch. The judge's output is validated by a schema either way, so a weaker or slower node fails loudly instead of quietly writing a wrong verdict. If you are building on a decentralized inference network, you cannot assume the same model, the same latency or the same token limits on every call. Designing the agent so that the model is the least trusted part is how you get repeatable results anyway. What broke, honestly The hackathon asked for building blocks tested and lessons learned, and these were the useful ones: Read-only tools still asked for confirmation. A tool tagged read_only and idempotent=True still came back as "Policy confirmation required ... reply yes", because the decorator default min_scope="WRITE_SAFE" wins over the tags. Declaring min_scope="READ_ONLY" fixed it. The first request of every turn was not my…

articles.title: Uncommon Thinkers: Alexis Harroun aims for space with a new engine — and stays grounded
articles.content: Juno Propulsion co-founder and CEO Alexis Harroun is working on rotating detonation engines at her startup. (Juno Propulsion Photo) Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners . A few weeks after learning that her tiny startup had won a NASA prize to fly its engine in space, Alexis Harroun was camping in Yellowstone, sitting around a fire and looking up at the stars. Satellites kept drifting past overhead — and the news finally sank in. “I’m like, oh, we’re going to be sending something up and we’re going to be able to see it,” she said. “That was very humbling in a lot of ways and very exciting.” Harroun is co-founder and CEO of Juno Propulsion , a Tukwila, Wash.-based startup building a new kind of rocket engine. Instead of burning fuel in a steady flame, Juno’s engines use detonation, a supersonic combustion wave that releases more energy from the same amount of propellant. “It’s essentially like a higher MPG rocket engine,” Harroun said. The technology has been studied for decades but has never flown in orbit. Juno aims to change that next year, when its engine is set to fly aboard a Momentus satellite in a mission called Project Iris . That’s a big goal for a company that, when the July 2025 NASA call came , was just Harroun, co-founder and CTO Ari Martinez and a summer intern working out of a one-room office. If Iris succeeds, Juno’s engines could let satellites run on non-toxic fuel and maneuver far more freely in orbit, something both commercial and defense customers increasingly want. For Harroun, who earned her Ph.D. studying these engines, it would be the payoff of years of work. Harroun sees the technology as a long-overdue leap. The basic physics behind today’s rocket engines dates to the 1930s and has been refined about as far as it can go, she said, calling it a constraint that’s “been a glass ceiling for too long, in my opinion.” No astronaut story Harroun grew up south of Seattle in Federal Way. She didn’t come from an aerospace family or spend her childhood dreaming about space. Her dad was a physician and her mom a flight attendant and flight instructor. What she did pick up at home was an entrepreneurial streak. Her dad ran his own practice for about 20 years, and her mom is now a real estate agent. Harroun said watching them make “something out of completely nothing” has shaped her own path, especially in building Juno. She calls herself a “late bloomer” who fell for engineering as she was finishing high school and heading to the University of Washington. Sci-fi became an inspiration along the way, and it’s now one of her favorite genres. She spent all four years at UW working with professor Carl Knowlen , who leads the Aeronautics & Astronautics Department’s Detonation Engines Lab, and she joined the student rocketry team, eventually leading its propulsion group. Knowlen “sees the potential in everyone,” Harroun said, and the two built a strong relationship that’s still going. Juno’s $1.2 million National Science Foundation grant , awarded this summer, is a partnership with his research group. “What’s exciting is seeing this come full circle,” Knowlen said in a 2025 UW story . “Alexis’s passion for this technology grew out of our lab work together, and now we’re collaborating to turn that early research into something that will fly in space.” Working on a engine in the University of Washington Department of Aeronautics & Astronautics, from left: Professor Carl Knowlen, Juno intern Ben Cabot, Alexis Harroun, Ariana Martinez and A&A graduate student Ben Fetters. (UW Photo) During college, Harroun interned at NASA, Boeing and Blue Origin. That first stint at Blue Origin, in 2016, set her next move. “I realized that everyone who had the job that I wanted had gone to Purdue,” she said. She spent the next six years at Purdue University in West…
