articles.title: ‘A huge pain in the ass’: Microsoft 365 starts to recover after a day of global email turmoil
articles.content: Microsoft says delayed email is close to cleared after an outage that cut off Outlook for much of Thursday. ( Unsplash Photo / Ed Hardie ) Updated at 4 p.m. PT Nov. 13 with additional Microsoft statements. If emails sent by Outlook users on Thursday are just now landing in your inbox, no, you haven’t gone back to the days of the Pony Express. Microsoft is still digging out from a nearly daylong outage that cut off email for businesses, schools and governments around the world. As of early Friday, the company reported that email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels,” though some users could still have trouble getting in or see delayed messages. In a post on X Friday morning, Microsoft said it was “deeply sorry” for the disruption to customers and partners. The company said the outage was a technical issue, not related to a cyberattack or AI agents. The problem was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade and surfaced after a more recent network change, the company said, adding that it has addressed the underlying issue and is still restoring service to remaining customers and regions. We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services. This was a technical issue… — Microsoft (@Microsoft) November 13, 2026 In an update on its status page at 5 a.m. Pacific, Microsoft said it was seeing “broader improvements now observed in North America and sustained improvements across much of Europe,” along with early signs of recovery in Asia Pacific. The problems started Thursday morning with Exchange Online, the Microsoft service that runs Outlook email for businesses, and spread to other Microsoft 365 services that depend on it, including Teams calendars, Copilot and SharePoint. Microsoft said servers were failing automated health checks and dropping out of service, which overloaded the ones that were left. The company paused all deployments while it worked on a fix, and some of its repairs Thursday evening were “not taking as expected.” Microsoft said it restored service gradually, checking stability at each stage, which took longer but helped ensure a stable restoration. Earlier, The Verge’s Tom Warren reported on X that his sources linked the outage to configuration changes in Azure Virtual Network, Microsoft’s cloud networking service. Australia’s Home Affairs Minister, Tony Burke, told reporters in Sydney that Microsoft believes it is dealing with something similar in some ways to the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, “where there is an update that has gone awry,” the Associated Press reported . “We know our customers rely on our services to get important work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us,” said Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, in a statement provided to GeekWire. He said Microsoft’s teams are reviewing what happened and how to prevent similar problems. In a post on X Friday afternoon, Lamanna said the investigation points to “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter,” which made recovery harder than normal. A thundering herd happens when large numbers of clients try to reconnect at the same time, overwhelming systems as they come back online. He said Microsoft will publish a post-mortem “shortly” with a step-by-step timeline and the repairs it plans to make to avoid similar outages. The outage reached well beyond email. Government offices in Japan, Singapore and the Philippines reported disruptions, according to the AP. Workhorse Group delayed its quarterly earnings call, and OpenAI and Anthropic both reported problems connecting with Microsoft…

articles.title: Here’s how to teach AI agents to search like human experts
articles.content: Agentic retrieval is a hot topic for a reason: Every company wants to automate work, but they often just are not ready. It’s also extremely easy — and tempting — to spin up an agent, point it at a mountain of data, and spend heavily on tokens for a lackluster result. To unleash agents that can accomplish work, you’ll need a different approach. You can’t throw a more intelligent AI model at a failing agentic workflow without first sorting out how to provide it with better data. It won’t do much good. So how should companies prepare their information for quick, accurate agentic use? That’s what The New Stack will be digging into live with Vespa.ai ’s Jenny Morris on Wednesday, December 2. articles.title: Introducing Spend Management: Spending limits and alerts for Cloudflare
articles.content: Spend controls have been at the top of the list of most requested features from developers building on our developer platform for quite some time now. With more than 10 million developers now building on Cloudflare, this matters more than ever. Although we’ve had usage notifications and budget alerts available to paid plans for a while, this doesn’t solve the problem completely; informing is not the same as controlling. You can now set spending thresholds and choose to have Cloudflare pause activity when those limits are reached, thus avoiding unexpected bills from unplanned usage. Today, we're introducing Spend Management in Beta, for any pay-as-you-go (PayGo) customer, starting with Workers and Durable Objects. Use Spend Management alongside AI Gateway spend limits to manage compute and AI inference costs across your application. AI Gateway already supports per-user and per-model budgets for Workers AI and other AI providers, applied to requests routed through your gateway. How it works You can start using Spend Management using the dashboard, cf CLI , or REST API . In the dashboard , head over to Manage Account > Billing > Spend limits and enable the products for which you want to control spending. When you enable controls on a product, you can define a spending limit, specify a recipient email for notifications, and set one or more alert thresholds. If you configure a recipient email, Cloudflare will send notifications when the evaluated spend reaches one of the thresholds or your spending limit. When the limit is reached, a blocking policy is enforced and your product is paused automatically. If you go to the dashboard , you can see the current billing cycle costs for each supported product in near real time (under 10 minutes), and manage your settings and thresholds from there. The overview panel tells you which products have thresholds and limits configured. In this example, you can see that Workers triggered two alerts before hitting the hard limit. Note that the billing cycle starts when the paid subscription begins, not when you deploy a Worker or create a spending cap; a subscription starting October 10 generally has a cycle of October 10-November 10 — not a calendar month. The dashboard also shows an audit log, so you can see who changed a limit and when, or when a cap was reached. As with most Cloudflare services, Spend Management is also an API that you can use programmatically; the documentation can be found in our Developer Documentation . Here’s an example, but using the API: curl --fail-with-body --request POST \ "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/${CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID}/billing/spend-policies" \ --header "Authorization: Bearer ${CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN}" \ --header "Content-Type: application/json" \ --data '{ "name": "Workers spending cap", "product_id": "workers", "enabled": true, "threshold_cents": 10000, "action": "usage_block", "notification_email": "me@example.com" }' And, of course, you can use cf, the CLI for the entire Cloudflare API : cf billing spend-policies list cf billing spend-policies create cf billing spend-policies get cf billing spend-policies update cf billing spend-policies delete cf billing spend-policies audit list cf billing spend-policies activity list cf billing spend-policies create --body '{ "name": "Workers spending cap", "product_id": "workers", "enabled": true, "threshold_cents": 10000, "action": "usage_block", "notification_email": "me@example.com" }' Once a cap is enforced, new invocations of that product are rejected. Note that we only pause customer-code invocations that incur costs — in Workers, for example, Cron Triggers and Queue consumer invocations are paused, but static assets continue to be served. To resume service, you can: Raise the limit above the current cycle’s accumulated spend. Disable or delete the blocking policy. Wait until the next billing cycle, when the existing block expires. That’s it. You can start using Spend Management for Workers…

articles.title: This Houston startup is using old oil wells to make clean hydrogen
articles.content: Deep in West Texas, an old oil field is nearing the end of its commercial life. But a startup recently spent a month at the site producing a new energy source: clean, ultra low-carbon hydrogen. Eclipse , the startup, uses microbes to break down oil in end-of-life wells, releasing hydrogen that can be brought to the surface using existing infrastructure. In the pilot, the company generated hydrogen for 30 days straight before stopping the test. But the company says that old oil field projects like this have the potential to produce hydrogen for 10-20 years—and can make it cheap enough that it could be used to produce clean, baseload power for the electric grid. There’s an abundant supply of hydrogen in oil fields. “When you produce these oil fields, you’re lucky if you produce 40% of the oil,” says Eclipse’s CEO, Prabhdeep Singh Sekhon, who previously worked in the oil and gas industry. “There’s still a tremendous amount of hydrocarbon in the ground; it’s just not economic to produce. If there’s hydrocarbon, that also inherently means there’s also hydrogen.” Mining old oil fields for clean energy Other approaches to clean hydrogen have struggled. The promise is big: Hydrogen emits only water vapor when it’s burned, and it could slash emissions in everything from steel production to ships . But it’s hard to make affordably. Green hydrogen, which uses renewable electricity to split water, is expensive and water intensive. Hydrogen is traditionally made with natural gas, and it’s also expensive to capture carbon in that approach. “Natural” or geologic hydrogen, which looks for reservoirs of hydrogen that are trapped underground, hasn’t yet proven that it’s viable. Turning to old oil wells could help. Microbes are the key to unlocking the hydrogen. Eclipse built a huge database of microbes found in oil fields, and created its own mix of the microbes to capture the hydrogen from the oil remaining in abandoned wells. The company injects microbes into reservoirs, where the microbes “eat” the oil and release hydrogen gas. (It’s worth noting that the process also releases CO2; the company says that some CO2 stays underground, and emissions can be captured.) Hydrogen, a lightweight molecule, flows through the reservoirs and can be produced through the wells that are in place. In the pilot, when the company injected microbes in one well, the hydrogen also flowed to a second well around 600 feet away. The company performed a smaller pilot last year in California, but says that the Texas pilot proves that the process works under more challenging geological and chemical conditions. Unlike natural hydrogen, the approach doesn’t require expensive exploration. It’s already clear where the hydrogen is. And it can use existing infrastructure. “You have billions of dollars in a field that’s already been deployed—the wells are drilled, the surface facilities are installed, the [rights-of-way] are there,” says Sekhon. That reduces the time to deploy a project, he says, along with the cost of production. The underlying technology still needs to be optimized for commercial use. Scaling up could be a challenge, says Geoffrey Ellis, a researcher who studied geologic hydrogen at the U.S. Geological Survey and now teaches at Stanford. But “the resource potential is enormous,” he says. “There’s a lot of hydrocarbons in the subsurface that are unrecoverable. If we can convert that economically into hydrogen, that would be a game changer.” From data centers to fertilizer The approach is appealing for oil and gas companies, since old oil fields that would otherwise be a liability—with wells that have to be plugged and abandoned—can suddenly find a new life. “For an operator, a field that’s about to become a cost can become a source of revenue, its productive life is extended, and plugging costs are pushed out,” says Depinder Sandhu, executive VP and chief commercial officer of Weatherford, an oil field…

articles.title: Apple's canceled iOS multitasking UI lives on, with AI-enhanced emulation
articles.content: An unreleased iPhone multitasking interface, unseen for over a decade and a half, was brought back to life with the help of AI and emulation. An unreleased Expose-like multitasking design has surfaced once again, with the help of AI. Before the iPhone got the app switcher we all know and love, Apple made multitasking available through a sliding drawer that popped up at the bottom of the screen. However, the company experimented with a much more impressive design, showing open apps as on-screen cards. After AppleInsider described an Expose-like interface in early 2010 , a special build of iOS 4 was discovered on an iPhone 4 prototype the very next year. In the decade that followed, nobody had ever showcased the card-like multitasking design - until an emulator developer used AI to bring the scrapped UI back to life. Continue Reading on AppleInsider | Discuss on our Forums

articles.title: Robot Talk Episode 170 – Robots in the real world, with Daniela Shchegelskaya
articles.content: Claire chatted to Daniela Shchegelskaya from the University of Twente about getting robots to operate reliably in safety-critical environments. Daniela Shchegelskaya is an electronics and robotics engineer specialising in autonomous systems, control engineering, and Al-driven robotics for industrial and safety-critical environments. She works on deploying real-world autonomous robots beyond lab conditions, focusing on reliability, connectivity, and system-level design. At Elimpus, she works on the integration of Boston Dynamics’ Spot for inspections in live power substations, including autonomous navigation, network connectivity, remote diagnostics, data collection and system-level reliability.

articles.title: ‘Broken and shattered’ Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang surrendered during resignation meeting, report claims
articles.content: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has reportedly called himself “a piece of sh**" as he left the company he built over 33 years. Bloomberg reports that the co-founder, known for his legendary energy and outgoing demeanor, surrendered and looked “broken and shattered” during the board meeting where he resigned from the AI hardware firm after admitting to at least one extra-marital affair , including one with a suspected Chinese spy . But despite his resignation and the controversies surrounding him, it seems that Nvidia employees are still rallying behind him, with thousands of comments on the company’s internal “suggestion box” showing support for the disgraced leader, according to Wired . “If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” one commenter said, while another one wrote, “We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance.” An Nvidia staffer told Wired privately, “Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen,” even as another employee sent a company-wide email demanding transparency into his resignation. “I stand by Jensen. Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.” They also added, “If America fails the man who helped build its future, then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.” According to the report, internal calls for Huang's reinstatement have drawn more than 1,600 comments on Nvidia's internal forums, "the majority in full support of reinstalling him." The company has more than 42,000 employees worldwide. Rumors about Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy, being close to Jensen Huang first circulated in late October, with Nvidia vehemently denying there was any impropriety. “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” an Nvidia spokesperson told Tom's Hardware . However, things took a turn for the worse for the Nvidia CEO when reports came out that he actually had an affair with Ms. Huang . Nvidia General Counsel and Secretary of the Board Tim Teter confronted Jensen at his house when this came out, after which he confessed. The founder soon released a statement admitting to and apologizing for his actions , while the company’s board formed an independent committee to investigate. However, another scandal broke out revealing that the former Nvidia chief had another affair — this time with a subordinate. This was apparently the last straw for the board, and the Nvidia co-founder was forced to resign soon after . Reports say that Jensen Huang was a hands-on leader, with over 60 executives at the company reporting directly to him, and that he was known to respond to emails quickly, whether it was day or night. But, more importantly, he was the face of the company who was particularly loved by many people, giving rise to the term “Jensanity” in his home country of Taiwan . Regardless of his status as a billionaire, people still find him trying out street food , eating at fast food chains , and even honoring his humble beginnings as a busboy at Denny’s . Aside from these latest scandals, many gamers castigate Huang for abandoning the core market that supported Nvidia before it became an AI giant, with consumer graphics cards now drastically more expensive than ever before. He was also often criticized for his all-out push on artificial intelligence and stance on selling chips to China . Still, those issues did not detract from his aura, with his trademark leather jacket raising nearly $1 million at a charity auction. It remains to be seen what will happen to Jensen after his monumental fall from grace, with SpaceX and Tesla mogul Elon Musk noting it would be an honor to hire Huang.
articles.author: Jowi Morales

articles.title: The Download: Silicon Valley’s blind spot and Nvidia’s chip-tracking plan
articles.content: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong? —Aaron Zamost, a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley have built careers claiming to see the future. Yet five weeks before the midterms, many gathered at the White House to pose with Trump and endorse his “Super Intelligence” agenda, despite growing opposition to AI and data centers. Their decision to lash themselves to President Trump was a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment. Here’s why Silicon Valley’s tech leaders may be less visionary than they think . Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility Nvidia representatives told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it was possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review on Thursday, despite an industry group claiming they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips and prevent their smuggling to China. The act is drawing renewed attention following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair. Find out what the proposed tracking measures would involve . —James O’Donnell More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can control robotic limbs and computers, and even “speak.” The people who volunteer for trials of these devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart, who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014. He’s been working on a set of guidelines for ethical trials to respect participants’ autonomy—and access their own brain data whenever they want. Read the full story on the push to give volunteers in brain implant trials more rights . —Jessica Hamzelou This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. articles.title: How AI Is Helping Care Teams Get Patients the Right Care, Sooner
articles.content: From pediatric research to smart hospitals, AI is helping care teams spend less time on routine tasks and more time with patients. Health systems and startups are putting it to work across healthcare, from matching patients to clinical trials to supporting radiologists, hospital teams and patients at home. Clinicians stay at the center, reviewing AI outputs and guiding decisions, while NVIDIA technologies provide the compute behind the applications. Read on to learn how healthcare teams are using AI to improve and speed patient care. Friday, Nov. 13, 5:00 a.m. PT Dyania Health Uses AI to Turn Decades of Patient Records Into Better Care Hospitals hold decades of patient history, most of it written in free text, as physicians’ notes, operative reports, imaging and pathology reads and discharge summaries. To understand one patient’s full story, a clinician would need to read through years of charts . Dyania Health , a New Jersey-based clinical AI company, built Synapsis AI to do just that. Synapsis AI is a clinical reasoning engine: It works across every note, report and lab result in a patient’s record, connecting findings that may be years apart to answer clinical questions the way a specialist reviewing the chart would. The output is a set of clinical signals, each traceable to its source in the record, that tells care teams which patients need attention and why. Clinicians review the evidence and make every decision. Keeping Patient Data Inside the Hospital Walls Synapsis AI runs on NVIDIA-accelerated computing inside a health system’s own firewall. The entire health system’s patient records can be processed onsite, so patient data is never shared and never leaves the hospital. Processing records this way takes chart review off the desks of clinical teams and lets them spend that time with patients. But Synapsis AI still requires clinician input — it’s an assistive tool that surfaces evidence from medical records that a clinician must still confirm and act on. Dyania builds and trains its clinical models with NVIDIA NeMo open libraries, then uses NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM to optimize them to run faster and more efficiently on the hospital’s own GPU servers. Synapsis AI in the Real World Cleveland Clinic used Synapsis AI to support a study of more than 7,800 aortic valve replacement patients between 2005 and 2021. Synapsis AI reasoned across each patient’s record, including every echocardiogram added in the years after surgery, and used this information to build a predictive model of valve deterioration and reintervention risk at the three-, five- and ten-year mark after a patient undergoes an aortic valve replacement procedure. The AI platform completed chart review across the full cohort that would have taken clinicians years to complete by hand. “Using technology to bring together and analyze information that can help us predict the duration of implanted heart valves is a promising step towards enhanced outcomes and more personalized care for patients,” said Dr. Lars Svensson , chief of the Heart, Vascular & Thoracic Institute at Cleveland Clinic. The same approach can be applied to any healthcare challenge where the answer sits inside the medical record, such as identifying patients eligible for clinical trials, closing care gaps in cardiology and oncology, and populating clinical registries. Learn more about Dyania Health .

articles.title: Japanese workers return to fax machines during ongoing Microsoft 365 outage
articles.content: Japanese workers dealing with the impacts of Microsoft's ongoing 365 outage have reportedly taken to analog measures, including using fax machines to deal with the ongoing blackout, the Japan Times reports. An outage that has now lasted nearly 24 hours was still going on Friday when employees turned up to work. The downtime has meant businesses reliant on Microsoft 365 are unable to use Outlook, Teams, and Copilot, with workplaces hit with error messages and blank screens, forced to reschedule meetings or delay work. For some, the outage has proven a respite from Japan's notoriously workaholic culture. "I couldn’t open Outlook and panicked … I got in touch with my boss and was told to stay home," one person reported on X, while another remarked that the only task they could carry out at work was to clean the coffee machine in the production room. But while some employees and companies are throwing in the towel and calling it an early weekend, others are taking a novel, more analog approach. "Microsoft’s server glitch has made it impossible to get any work done since this morning. I guess phones and fax machines really are unbeatable. … We’re going full analog!" one user claimed. The report cites another employee who confirmed that their company was switching to fax machines to send the regular updates the company normally sends out as PDFs. "Analog is strong," they rejoiced. Some 78% of Japanese companies rely on Microsoft for their digital infrastructure. The outage began on Thursday, with mass disruption to Outlook, Teams, Copilot, OneDrive, and Microsoft 365 as a whole. It's a saga impacting entire sectors, including UK health care, businesses, travel, and transport. Microsoft's latest update said it was seeing "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe, while the situation in America was improving, but warned some users may still experience intermittent issues. The company has also denied rumblings that the outage was caused by a cybersecurity breach. The outage has even caused some companies, such as Switzerland's luxury Richemont (Cartier) outfit, to delay giving their latest earnings report.
articles.author: Stephen Warwick

articles.title: Microsoft is winding down its Oracle deal. It could be a sign of what’s to come
articles.content: In late September, news circulated that the hyperscaler Oracle had sent a force majeure notice to the developer of its New Mexico data center campus, Project Jupiter, seeking to delay payments on the project should it fail to come on line in 2028 as planned. In response, Oracle took to X, writing that “force-majeure notices are commonplace in developments of this scale. They do not, by themselves, establish a project delay or change delivery expectations.” The hiccup was one in a series. According to Financial Times reporting from September , loans tied to the project had been “privately quoted at 89 to 91 cents on the dollar by syndicated banks like Santander and Jefferies,” reflecting, more broadly, Oracle’s barely-above-junk credit rating and its place as the company to watch for those who are concerned about an AI bubble bursting soon. That fact is made crystal clear by both press surrounding the subject and the strength of the market for Oracle credit-default swaps (essentially insurance against Oracle defaulting on its debt). Things have since gotten worse for Oracle. Last week, overlooked by many amid the midterms and unfolding drama at Nvidia , the Financial Times reported that Oracle canceled an estimated $7 billion chip deal with the Chinese tech giant Tencent under pressure from the Trump administration. Two days later, Bloomberg reported that Microsoft had been winding down a 2023 deal to rent AI computing from Oracle that had originally been arranged to meet the computing demands of its Copilot AI assistant. Microsoft reportedly walked away because Oracle’s Nvidia chips were already outdated—a growing concern for investors financing expensive AI infrastructure that risks becoming obsolete before it can pay for itself. As one fund manager put it colorfully to the Financial Times : “It’s like financing a fax machine and then someone invented email.” If Microsoft was in fact dissatisfied with the chips, this marks one of the more significant manifestations of the chip-lifecycle concern, which so far has seemingly lived in analysts’ forecasts. It also bears out the problem of mismatched timelines. Oracle is operating on decade-plus horizons, in one sense, with its data center development. But the pressure to meet short-term obligations with big swings and the need for labs to develop their frontier models mean that the build-out goings-on are happening in large part on very different timelines—year to year or even month to month. Oracle predictably pushed back on X , saying demand for its AI infrastructure remains strong, even for older Nvidia chips. The company said that in its first quarter (which runs from June through August), it renewed or resold capacity using GPUs that were mostly at least four years old, securing long-term contracts at a 20% premium over previous pricing. While it might seem that Oracle is continuously and unnecessarily sticking its neck out on social media to combatively address every single concern about its financing practices, the company’s posting habits make sense in an environment characterized by rising interest rates and reemergent concern about the AI bubble. Oracle has financed its build-out with more leverage than its peers and similarly negative cash flow. And it’s failed to quell concerns about its borrowing. Earlier this month, it burned through the entire $20 billion fundraising cap meant to last through fiscal 2030, just five days after announcing it. And it’s not only the leverage itself that has watchers concerned—or, doubly the economic consequences of the war in Iran—but also electoral politics. Compounding Oracle’s troubles are two broader threats to the AI build-out: a growing political backlash against data centers and mounting investor anxiety over infrastructure spending. In the midterms, voters approved 40 of 41 ballot measures aimed at restricting data center construction. In New Mexico, Governor-elect Deb Haaland pledged to impose a moratorium on new…

articles.title: Protein Startups Are Selling Lots Of Snacks And Drinks. Our Sample Tasting Found Most Neither Great Nor Horrible
articles.content: In a perfect world, we would all eat meals and snacks that are convenient, taste great and provide optimal nutrition. In reality, however, there are tradeoffs. We crave ice cream, chips and candy bars, which make carbs and fat easy to over-consume. Meeting protein goals, meanwhile, can require conscientious effort, particularly for those, like your author, who aren’t keen on eating lots of meat. Fortunately, as we chronicled earlier this week , both startups and established food brands are making it simpler than ever to up protein intake. From sodas to snack bars to ice cream, it’s now possible to get a fix of this coveted macronutrient with foods and drinks more commonly associated with sugar, starch and fat. The looming question is: Do they taste good? To find out, we hit up a local Target for a selection of protein foods sold by venture-backed startups. I and a 10-year-old then subjected them to a taste test. The verdict? Most of this stuff is indeed edible and drinkable, albeit almost never nearly as tasty as the more protein-deficient alternatives, with just one exception. Our findings below: No. 1: David Vanilla Bean Frozen Dessert : Anyone who buys or consumes this particular ice cream alternative will be doing so for the nutritional content, not the taste. A single pint packs in a whopping 30 grams of protein and has just 210 calories. The texture is also on point, creamy and easy to spoon, with a distinct vanilla flavor. That said, you can’t hide the fact that this is not a product made with your typical ice cream ingredients. Those who don’t like artificial sweeteners or the flavor and texture of whey protein will want to pass. For myself and my co-taster, however, it was a reasonably appealing eating experience. Not as good as traditional ice cream, but not bad for a high-protein food. Made by: Medici Brands ( David parent company). No. 2 SkyPop Protein Soda : The nutritional stats for SkyPop Protein Soda are also remarkable. A 12-ounce can has just 45 calories, with 10 grams of protein and a single gram of carbohydrates. It’s also properly fizzy, and makes a satisfying pop when you open the can. But what about flavor? Our local store only had the Ice Pop flavor in stock and it was, in both tasters’ view, not horrible but not something we’d plan to buy regularly. I could see consuming it when on a clear fluids diet, as is the case before some medical procedures, as it’d be one of the few available sources of protein. Made by: SkyPop (formerly Don’t Quit) No. 3: Khloud Protein Popcorn : Unlike many of our other featured foods, Khloud Protein Popcorn isn’t a super protein-rich offering. A serving contains 7 grams of protein and 160 calories, most of which come from carbs and fat. Still, its protein count is higher than other packaged popcorn, which typically has maybe 2 protein grams in a comparable serving. Overall, the tasters’ conclusion, from our trial of White Cheddar Khloud, was that this is a decent snack food. The flavor of milk protein and whey protein concentrate was palpable, but not overwhelming. It’s not exactly a snack food to savor, but for something to casually munch at one’s desk or while watching a show, it served its purpose. Made by: Khloud No. 4 Mosh : In the third season of “The White Lotus”, Mosh co-founder Patrick Schwarzenegger plays a fitness and finance bro who makes a daily high-protein shake that other family members find revolting. Perhaps this was inspired by Mosh, the brain-supporting protein bar startup he launched with his mother, Maria Shriver . The Mosh bar, which we purchased in the peanut butter cup flavor, crams 20 grams of protein, 6 grams of fiber, plus brain-supporting ingredients like creatine and lion’s mane, into a compact, shelf-stable bar. It’s an impressive feat. Yet while our brains’ may have appreciated the nutrition and supplement boost the Mosh bar provided, our taste buds decidedly did not. I’d put Mosh in the functional food category. It’s something that you…

articles.title: How the U.S.’s biggest news union is fighting an AI onslaught
articles.content: A decade ago, while working as a data reporter at the Los Angeles Times , Jon Schleuss watched a new boss take control of the paper’s parent company, rename it Tronc, and promise to supercharge the business by repackaging the paper’s “content” across an array of media. Instead, leadership began “running it into the ground,” says Schleuss. “We decided to fight.” He soon helped organize the newsroom’s first union. Now, as president of the NewsGuild-CWA, the largest news union in the United States, Schleuss is hearing a new version of the same story, this time powered by AI. Case in point: USA Today Co., formerly Gannett, the country’s largest newspaper chain. In August, the company announced a partnership with Palantir—the data analytics giant whose clients include Nvidia , U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE ), and Britain’s National Health Service—to better monetize its audience and content. It’s part of a broader effort that includes push-button videos, AI-written article summaries, and even whole articles. That sort of automation echoes moves across the media industry. NewsGuild members at USA Today papers have demanded an end to the Palantir deal, citing reader trust and a conflict of interest for reporters who cover ICE. The union has also pushed back on some of the company’s artificial intelligence initiatives amid continuing layoffs. Last month, after the rollout of a new reader-facing chatbot across USA Today websites, guild journalists at two papers in Ohio pulled their bylines; among its hallucinations , they said, the bot misidentified the reporter covering a murder case as the suspect. In a September interview , Mike Reed, the USA Today CEO, told Fast Company that the company won’t replace journalists with AI. But unlike Ziff Davis, IGN , The New Republic , Time , and CalMatters , Schleuss says, it hasn’t put that promise in a contract—something that NewsGuild journalists are now demanding in ongoing negotiations. Still, the layoffs keep coming , even in some cases when those protections are in place. The Local Journalist Index estimates that the U.S. has lost about 80% of its local journalists since the turn of the century, from about 40 per 100,000 residents in 2002 to just 7.8 today. All the upheaval is fueling an organizing surge, one Schleuss says the union hasn’t seen since its founding in 1933 as the American Newspaper Guild, during the Great Depression. In the time that he has been president, the guild has added more than 10,000 workers from 246 workplaces—not just journalists but people in the publishing, tech, and nonprofit worlds. (Reporters at Fast Company and Inc. unionized with the Writers Guild of America East in 2018.) “You see CEOs that make millions of dollars and don’t increase your pay and want to lay you off and speak in this weird, AI-written code-speak,” Schleuss says. “It tends to tick people off when the price of groceries is just through the roof.” Schleuss spoke with Fast Company about the industry’s embrace of AI, the growing labor movement in journalism, and what it will take to protect reporters—and the work they do. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Jon Schleuss at a Washington Post Tech Guild rally, April 2025. [Photo: Courtesy Jon Schleuss] Generative AI is being rolled out all over the place, from healthcare to hiring to scammy content creating . Why is the discussion about AI in journalism so critical? The news industry is the only industry mentioned in the Constitution—we can start there. A free press is essential to having a democracy, and so if you replace the workers who provide that free press with bots, you get misinformation. Our currency is trust. And you can’t do that if you’ve got corporations that are just spewing out word calculators to replace those working journalists who have ethical responsibilities: seeking truth and reporting it, minimizing harm,…

articles.title: BOFH: The best way to stop an idea spreading is a controlled burn
articles.content: Look, off in the ether – is it a bird, is it a plane? No, it's a stupid idea, on final approach... And look, the Boss has his office door open! C L E A R A N C E T O L A N D ! ... The Boss has wandered into Mission Control with something obviously on his mind. Over time, the PFY and I have learned to equate these thoughtful moments with the BAG FULL lamp of a commercial vacuum cleaner at a waxing salon. Do not open. His presence in Mission Control is never a good sign, but his "thoughtful" presence, even more so. He'll have seen something, read something, spoken to someone, or possibly overheard something in a toilet stall that will have sounded – to him – like a great idea. Or it might have been a cheddar-frenzy-induced fever dream that he wants to run by us. And the Boss's crazy ideas are, unfortunately, like bran flakes to his mental digestion, the output of which being delivered to the PFY and myself as a veritable slurry of poorly considered ideas. "AI," he says, pausing for effect, once he's rolled to a stop. He then waits patiently for one of us to ask "What about AI?" However, that will never happen. In terms of stupidity, it's up there with saying Candyman into a mirror five times, power washing a gremlin, or visiting a basement when Jason's in town. ... "For the security system," the Boss teases. I continue my intense focus on my monitors, hoping the lunacy will depart. The PFY does the same. The PFY and I know that the only way out of this is to stall till the end of the day, at which time the Boss's overnight reset will trigger, leaving him only a vague memory of having had a good idea. >clickety< >tap< "Uh-oh," I say, reaching into my drawer for my crashtop. "It looks like one of the distribution switches on 4 has crashed." >tappity< "And not just 4 – it looks like the boardroom has gone down too." "It could be a virus," I say, using words I know the Boss will respond to. "A virus?!" the Boss gasps. "I don't know. It's too soon to tell," I say, departing. ... So now I'm hiding in a cramped comms room on the fourth floor while I plug the crashtop into the CCTV VLAN so I can check on the Boss's location. Luckily, we upgraded the system to an AI-integrated platform, so I only need to type IDIOT into the search field to find him. Sure enough, he's back in his office, typing away furiously, which can only mean there's a memo on its way. And if there's a memo, there's a path to reminding him of his dumb idea tomorrow... >tappity< >tap< >tap< >clickety< On the screen, the Boss looks around anxiously as his laptop fires up DBAN in full confirm mode. He then reaches for a sheet of paper and starts scribbling furiously. >tappity< >tap< The office lights switch off as the BMS system clock suddenly finds out that it's midnight. On the screen, the Boss's phone torch comes on and he resumes scribbling. >bip< >bip< >bip< >biiiiiiip< >ring< "Hello?" the Boss asks, with a hint of feedback. "It's the virus!" I gasp. "It's coming from inside the building!!!" Meantime, I've messaged the PFY and advised him to pick up the shredder from the boardroom cupboard. "What do I do?" the Boss gasps. "It's the wireless broadband connection on the roof!" I say. "We need to disconnect it!" "I thought you said it was coming from inside the building?" the Boss asks. DAMMIT! >tappity< >click< >tap< >tap< Further discussion is impossible now that his phone is erasing itself, having been marked as a stolen device... The PFY was unable to find the shredder, as it looks to have been dumped now that board papers are no longer printed. On the plus side, he has a plan. ...two hours later... "So, we're clear to enter the building?" I ask the fire warden. "Yes, you're clear, though it looks like the fire started on your floor." "It doesn't surprise me," I say. "We're creative people. Our ideas spark innovation." "It looks like there was some as-yet-unknown accelerant used." "Really? Was it... enthusiasm?" I ask. "No, more like lighter fluid." "Oh," I say,…

articles.title: Garmin Enduro 4 review: monster MIP battery life makes this a value alternative to the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro
articles.content: Memory-in-pixel displays are becoming rarer on the best Garmin watches , but those who prefer them are still well served by the Enduro line. If battery life is your primary concern, the Enduro 4 delivers in spades. It lasted me 16+ days on a charge, around 50% longer than even the best sports watches with AMOLED displays for battery life, like the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro or Suunto Vertical 2. Garmin hasn’t held back on features either, with the Enduro 4 getting most of the same key sports tracking tools as the Fenix 9 Pro, in a lighter case and at a lower price. It’s an attractive package, but the elephant in the room is that the Enduro 3 is also getting nearly all the same new features as the Enduro 4 through software updates, has a similar design and the same incredible battery life, and undercuts the new watch in sales. Garmin Enduro 4 review: Price and availability (Image credit: Future) The Garmin Enduro 4 launched in October 2026 and costs $899 in the U.S. and £799 in the U.K. It’s the same launch price in the U.S. as the Enduro 3, but the latter is now available for £699/$799. It’s a cheaper alternative to the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro Solar, which is the MIP option of the Fenix line-up and starts at $1,099. Garmin Enduro 4 review: Design and display (Image credit: Future) The Garmin Enduro 4 is a large but lightweight watch that uses Garmin’s familiar five-button setup. It has a 51mm case and is thick, but being mostly made from plastic means it’s significantly lighter than the 51mm watch in the Fenix 9 line-up. It has a titanium bezel and a sapphire crystal screen with solar panels to boost the impressive battery life even further in sunny conditions. The memory-in-pixel display is clear enough to read in all conditions, though I do think the Enduro 4 is less bright and readable than Garmin’s AMOLED watches when indoors or under tree cover. (Image credit: Future) There are some hardware changes and improvements from the Enduro 3. The Enduro 4 has a silver bezel with fewer yellow highlights, and under the hood it has more RAM, a faster processor for maps, and double the storage (64GB vs. 32GB on the Enduro 3). The new watch also comes with Garmin’s new ComfortFit band, which I like a lot more than the UltraFit band that ships with the Enduro 3, though you can also buy the ComfortFit band separately. (Image credit: Future) On the top of the watch is a built-in flashlight with four brightness levels and a red mode, and on its underside is Garmin’s Elevate Gen 5 heart rate sensor, which is the same sensor as the Fenix 9 series and Enduro 3. While it’s not a diveproof watch like the Fenix 9, the Enduro 4 has a 10 ATM rating and is waterproof. It also lacks the mic and speaker you do get on the Fenix. Despite its size, I found the Enduro 4 comfortable to wear 24/7 throughout testing. It’s not as attractive as the all-titanium Fenix 9 Pro, but the Enduro 4 is still a good-looking watch to wear outside your training. Garmin Enduro 4 review: Sports tracking and training analysis (Image credit: Future) Unless you’re desperate to go diving, the Enduro 4 has all the customizable sports modes you could ever need to track your workouts, including the improved rucking and rowing modes introduced on the Fenix 9. Runners, cyclists, swimmers and triathletes get the most detail in their sports modes, including an improved stamina feature that aims to provide guidance on how much energy you have left in endurance activities and how best to pace them. The Enduro 4 feeds all the data you track during workouts into an extensive suite of training analysis tools. It has all the top-of-the-range features you get on the Garmin Forerunner 970 and Fenix 9, including running economy estimates (when paired with the Garmin HRM 600 chest strap) and ratings for overall endurance and hill-running ability. Garmin offers greater depth of training analysis than any other brand I’ve tested, and while you might not want or need all this data, it’s there if you do,…

articles.title: After BP monitoring smartwatches, HUAWEI reveals its first continuous glucose monitor
articles.content: Credit: Weibo / Huawei TL;DR HUAWEI has revealed a continuous glucose monitor in China. HUAWEI Sence G1 is the company’s first-ever Class III medical device. HUAWEI hasn’t shared details about availability but said it has been in development for over three years. HUAWEI may have been nearly wiped out of international markets by sanctions imposed on it during the first tenure of US President Donald Trump, but it remains at the top of China’s leaderboard. Along with its innovations across slab phones, foldables , and laptops —including laptops with foldable screens —HUAWEI also offers a broad range of wearables, including ones that monitor blood pressure . So far, the lineup has only comprised smartwatches and fitness bands, but HUAWEI is now adding a health-centric utility in the form of a glucose monitor. The HUAWEI Sence G1 is the company’s first continuous glucose monitor (CGM). The device works alongside other HUAWEI products, allowing users to view glucose levels on their phones, a smartwatch, or a HUAWEI fitness band. Besides monitoring a user’s glucose levels, the CGM will also alert them in case of any unusual spikes or dips.

articles.title: Is Mark Zuckerberg's cute new AI assistant a surveillance trap? Why child safety experts are sounding the alarm over Meta Muse
articles.content: Meta is already at the center of your online social life. Now, the company behind Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp wants a permanent spot on your desk. But Mark Zuckerberg’s latest products are triggering familiar red flags. Meta officially brands Muse AI as an 18+ productivity assistant. In reality, it looks more like a customizable toy. That cuddly, disarming design, paired with always-on microphones and ambient recording, is raising eyebrows. AI experts and children's digital safety campaigners speaking to TechRadar are warning that Muse AI and its upcoming Tamagotchi-style keychain companion, Muse Charm , create severe risks for children and teenagers. Following an initial rollout across the US and Canada in September, Meta’s new AI agent has begun to stretch its presence across Asia, landing in Japan , Singapore , and, soon, India . Now, despite the tech giant having yet to confirm a release date, reports suggest the company is eyeing Europe, with The Times revealing on Monday that the UK is first in line. As Muse edges closer to a global launch, is Meta’s new gadget setting the stage for the next youth privacy disaster? And are we ready to cope with the aftermath? Meta Muse: the cuteness trap (Image credit: Jacob Krol/Future) Already counting over 1.8 million daily users across the US and Canada, Muse is an AI agent that can carry out tasks on behalf of its users, like shopping online, booking vacations, or buying groceries. Muse Charm brings the AI agent into physical reality. The two-inch wearable hardware device reportedly has an OLED touchscreen, front and rear cameras, microphones, speakers, 5G connectivity, and USB-C charging, allowing users to talk to their Muse without needing to open their smartphone. At the visual center of the device is Jolly, a pink-cheeked, Labubu-style animated avatar that users can fully personalize — from its name, appearance, and outfits to its voice — transforming invisible software into a persistent, physical companion. While Mark Zuckerberg frames Jolly as a “fun, completely customizable character,” child safety advocates and behavioral researchers warn that this aesthetic functions as a psychological Trojan horse. Speaking to Fast Company , cuteness researcher Joshua Paul Dale notes that cute and child-like designs stimulate pleasure centers before users can evaluate risks, creating an instinctive urge to keep the device close. Moving beyond screen-based interactions, a wearable charm could then tap into innate social emotions, making conversations with ambient software feel as spontaneous and natural as speaking to a person standing beside you. That’s the warning coming from children's digital safety experts at the Canadian group The White Hatter , who note that such an always-on AI friend could fundamentally alter human attachment to the machine. Put simply, critics say that by leveraging nostalgia for Tamagotchis and popular designer toys, Meta is making a product capable of invasive surveillance feel harmless. Is the 18+ restriction a myth? AI safety specialist Kavya Pearlman — a former risk advisor during Meta’s Cambridge Analytica scandal — describes the toy-like aesthetic as a "deliberate attempt" to attract younger demographics. “This company has a lot of information that it knows will work towards gaining access to certain age groups,” she said. Meta, however, has so far rejected claims that Muse is directly targeting children. "This is a story in search of a story,” Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts told WIRED . Roberts insists the avatar customization simply brings users joy, while pointing out that the company requires everyone using the Muse app to provide their date of birth. When approached by TechRadar, a Meta spokesperson also explained that age checks will include analyzing links between users’ Muse accounts and their Facebook or Instagram accounts. In the absence of a clear signal that they’re over 18, a credit card verification will be required to keep using the…

articles.title: UK firms are spending billions on hidden infrastructure costs — money they can't spend on hiring or AI
articles.content: UK enterprises are overspending on infrastructure, and AI is making this more unpredictable AI platform and model licensing fees are more of an issue than token-based pricing models Companies are having to cut back on hiring and training as a result New research has revealed UK businesses are losing £3.8 billion every year to unexpected infrastructure costs – a figure that rises to £47.4 billion across the UK, US, Japan, Italy, Germany, France, Australian and New Zealand. And that's not the amount that businesses are spending on infrastructure – it's only the portion of cash being spend that they weren't expecting to spend, the study from Wasabi and the Centre for Economics and Business Research (CEBR) found. Around one-third (32%) of the overspending in the UK is attributed to AI and ML infrastructure, the research found, with one in five (22%) UK businesses describing this are of spending as 'unpredictable'. Unexpected infrastructure spend is eye-watering, and AI is making it unpredictable By far the highest infrastructure overspend category was AI platform and model licensing fees (66%), far ahed of token and usage-based charges (36%) even though the apparent ongoing shift from seat-based to consumption-based models has been criticized for making spend more unpredictable. The scale of overspend is also particularly alarming, because nearly three-quarters (73%) of businesses globally reported either a moderate or significant budget pressure. Three in four (77%) British companies have also had to make at least one cost-driven trade-off during the previous 12 months, including cutting new hires across tech roles (38%), limiting their tech investments (37%) or spending less on worker training schemes (34%). "This means hiring and investment in new technologies are postponed or reduced as budgets are redirected to cover unexpected charges," CEBR head of economics advisory Owen Good summarized. "[Businesses] are blindsided by unpredictable infrastructure costs that prevent them from driving their innovation agendas forward," Wasabi COO Marty Falaro added. CEBR modelling quantified these impacts, noting that recovered money otherwise overspent on infrastructure could actually be redirected to support over 8,200 jobs.
articles.author: Craig Hale

articles.title: I tested the DJI Osmo 360 II and Insta360 needs to be seriously scared
articles.content: “Uh oh,” is what Insta360 will doubtless have thought when the DJI Osmo 360 II launched. And it should’ve been worried. Up to now, Insta360 has been the undisputed king of 360 tech. But that reign has come to an end. It all comes down to one thing: 8K/60fps, which the DJI Osmo 360 II can shoot. The flagship Insta360 X6, meanwhile, cannot, topping out at 8K/50fps. Insta360 is simply not there yet with the tech, and in fairness, that’s understandable. 8K at 60fps in 360 degrees puts extreme demands on a pocket-sized camera, its processor, memory, battery and thermals. But somehow DJI has achieved it – which means it’s now ahead in the race. Even if the Osmo 360 II isn’t the best 360 camera in every area, it does the most important thing right now. It gives content creators the flexibility of 4K reframing from 360 footage at a frame rate fast enough for high-octane footage, and usable enough for YouTube. So should you buy this camera? Find out in my full DJI Osmo 360 II review. DJI Osmo 360 II review: Specs Starting price $699 / £509 Max video resolution 8K/60fps (360); 4K/120fps (Single lens) Sensors 2x 1/1.1-inch Stabilization Yes Screen 2-inch LED Internal memory 105GB MicroSD slot Yes Pre-recording Yes Wireless mic hookup Yes, via Bluetooth Wired mic hookup Yes Connectivity Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, USB-C Water resistance 33ft (10m) Battery 2,150 mAh Size 2.4 x 1.4 x 3.2 inches Weight 6.4 ounces DJI Osmo 360 II review: Price & availability (Image credit: Future) Unsurprisingly, given this is a flagship 360 camera, the Osmo 360 II isn’t cheap, opening the register at a whopping $699 in the U.S. at Amazon for the standard bundle with basic accessories. If you want accessories, the Adventure Combo I tested, with extra batteries and a selfie stick, costs $829 . Of course, this is thanks to U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods. It’s also worth noting that, resulting from its feud with the U.S. government, DJI has withdrawn first-party support in the States, meaning no care plans if the camera needs repair. In the U.K., the Osmo 360 II starts at £509 , which undercuts the Insta360 X6 by over £100. And U.K. consumers also get access to a wider range of accessories bundles at Amazon, so they can tailor their spend to exactly what they need. This pricing is comparable to the Insta360 X6, which also starts at $699. In my opinion, the 360 II is a much better buy thanks to the higher 60fps frame rate. In the U.K., where the 360 II is both more powerful and cheaper, it’s a total no-brainer. If you’re on a tighter budget, though, I’d advise checking out the Insta360 X5 ($549), GoPro MAX2 ($499) or the OG DJI Osmo 360 ($494). All shoot 8K 360 footage, just not at 60fps. DJI Osmo 360 II review: Design & controls (Image credit: Future) The Osmo 360 II is designed more or less the same as its predecessor. It looks the same, measures the same, and weighs the same. That means it’s a squat-looking thing, especially compared to the lankier X6. It isn’t small though, at 2.4 x 1.4 x 3.2 inches, nor is it light at 6.4 ounces, so if you’re after something more suited to mounting on a helmet, check out an action camera like the DJI Osmo Action 6 . Versus the OG Osmo 360, there have been no radical updates to the display, which still isn’t an OLED; no updates to the internal memory, which is still 105GB (although over double the X6’s 47GB); and no updates to waterproofing, which is rated at 33 feet (half the 66 feet of the X6). (Image credit: Future) The controls are essentially the same, with two buttons on the back for recording and mode changing, a power button, and most tweaks done via the menu system or app. I found the Osmo 360 II’s record button fiddly to press with gloves on. And while I like DJI’s menu, it’s a little busy-feeling on the small display — the X6’s bigger display makes it slightly easier to use in the heat of the moment. Overall though, no major complaints controls-wise. Mounting (Image credit: Future) The Osmo 360 II uses the same quick-release…

Enea, a telecom and cybersecurity software company based in Stockholm, found the group's attack sources in at least six Asian countries and named it SilentAir this week. articles.summaryEn: A newly identified spying group called SilentAir has used hacked equipment within Asian mobile operators to intercept the calls and texts of selected individuals, primarily in Taiwan. Enea, a Stockholm-based telecom and cybersecurity software company, identified attack sources in at least six Asian countries and assessed that SilentAir is a state-level actor.
insightsFa: گروه SilentAir با تجهیزات هک‌شده به اطلاعات حساس افراد دسترسی پیدا کرده است.
این حملات در حداقل شش کشور آسیایی شناسایی شده است.
بیشتر قربانیان این حملات در تایوان قرار دارند.
SilentAir به عنوان یک بازیگر دولتی شناسایی شده است.
اقدامات این گروه می‌تواند تهدیدی جدی برای امنیت کاربران باشد.
articles.whyItMattersFa: این خبر نشان‌دهنده تهدیدهای جدی امنیتی برای کاربران تلفن همراه در آسیا است و می‌تواند تأثیرات وسیعی بر حریم خصوصی و امنیت داده‌ها داشته باشد.
